Offices involved in emergency work will also remain open.
Bangladesh Bank will issue necessary instructions to keep banking activities operational during the holiday, while the Supreme Court will issue directives regarding court proceedings.
For private-sector industries, factories and establishments, the Ministry of Labor and Employment will issue necessary instructions regarding the general holiday in accordance with the Bangladesh Labor Act, 2006.

item.title: Tearful Scaloni says Argentina cannot replace Messi
item.description:
Argentina's coach, Lionel Scaloni, said that no one could take the place of Lionel Messi, speaking through tears after a 3-0 victory over Benin that marked Messi's departure from the national team.
For Scaloni, who won four major titles with Messi as his captain, the partnership was more than he had hoped for.
"It was truly like a dream come true," he said. "I never thought I could be the coach of the best player in history.”
His voice grew heavy as he went on. "We will be grateful to him forever for giving us the chance to be with him," he said.
"My eyes are watering, because there is so much going through my head right now," he said. "It will hurt not to see him anymore."
Under Scaloni, with Messi leading the team, Argentina won the 2021 Copa America, the 2022 World Cup, the 2022 Finalissima and the 2024 Copa America.
Messi scored once and set up two goals against Benin in his farewell match.
Asked about Argentina's future without Messi, Scaloni said there was no easy way to fill the void. Where, then, would the team find another Messi? "Nowhere," he said.
"We are working with young players now," he said. "This process will go on. But the feeling of having Messi next to you, nothing compares to it."
Scaloni tried to explain what made Messi different. "I have never seen such an aura in anyone else in my life," he said.
Then he seemed to remind himself of what had changed. "The player who could make a win possible in an impossible match with his extraordinary talent is no longer with you," he said.

item.title: Iyer hits ton as India hammer West Indies in T20 opener
item.description:
Captain Shreyas Iyer struck his maiden T20 international century to lead India to a convincing eight-wicket win over the West Indies in the opening match on Tuesday.
With India chasing 172 for victory, Iyer hit an unbeaten 102 off 43 balls to steer his team home with 32 balls to spare in Lucknow. India lead the five-match series 1-0.
With eight needed off 36 balls and Iyer on 95, Ishan Kishan handed his captain the strike and the top-order batter reached his ton with a six and then took a single to complete the chase.
Iyer and the T20 team produced the win after they landed in India on Monday evening with an Asian Games men's T20 gold medal.
While they were in Japan, a completely different India squad, led by Shubman Gill, beat West Indies 2-1 in an ODI series.
Swashbuckling Abhishek Sharma gave the hosts a brisk start in his 10-ball 21 before spinner Roston Chase got the left-hander caught out.
Left-arm spinner Akeal Hosein then struck in his 100th T20 for the West Indies to send back Sanju Samson caught and bowled for 11.
Iyer and the left-handed Kishan, who made 37, then took charge with a string of boundaries and put on an unbeaten stand of 137.
Iyer raised his first half-century off 28 balls after 10 T20 innings and then changed gear for his next set of 50 in 14 balls.
Spinners set up victory with debutant Naman Dhir returning figures of 3-31 to bowl out West Indies for 171.
India elected to field first and despite a quick start by skipper Shai Hope, who made 52 off 37 balls, the spinners struck regular blows.
Sherfane Rutherford top-scored with 56 but bowlers kept India in control.
Kuldeep Yadav and fellow spinner Axar Patel took two wickets each.
The second T20 is on Friday in Ranchi.

item.title: US beat Canada 1-0 to wrap up four-win international break
item.description:
US teen Justin Ellis scored the only goal as Mauricio Pochettino's young team ground out victory against Canada to cap a flawless international window with four wins from four friendlies.
The 1-0 win lacked the dynamism, fluidity and multiple goals of wins against Mexico, Chile and Peru, but was another vindication for Pochettino's policy of blooding fresh talent in the post-World Cup window.
Nineteen-year-old Ellis, who had scored on debut against Peru, bundled in an Alex Freeman strike midway through the first half, while Luc de Fougerolles came closest for Canada by hitting the crossbar after the break.
Ellis's goal was the only US shot on target, with a high-pressing Canada spending most of the game on the front foot but unable to break through.
Across four games, seven of 12 US goals were scored by teenagers, as Pochettino handed debuts to 13 new players in a major reset following his side's disappointing last-16 exit at this summer's home World Cup.
"I think it was perfect, the camp. The results were there," said Pochettino.
"I think if we keep that mentality, that mindset, everything is possible."
The US got off to a slow start, sitting deep and soaking up a barrage of fouls from an evidently motivated Canada team.
The Canadians had the early shots, though efforts from both Tani Oluwaseyi and Jacob Shaffelburg were from range and barely threatened.
A foul on teen Ellis outside the box prompted a bout of shoving between players, and Pochettino grew enraged on the sideline as the referee allowed several physical challenges to go unchecked.
Ellis was left limping badly but was determined to remain on the pitch, and his doggedness paid off.
In the 29th minute, Alex Freeman picked up the ball on the right flank, played a one-two with Malik Tillman, and surged into the box.
He appeared to shoot, but Ellis popped up to steer his wayward effort into the back of the net.
A slightly ill-tempered first-half ended with two yellow cards -- Oluwaseyi and Gio Reyna -- and Alex Freeman blazing a volley way over the crossbar.
Ellis was hooked at half-time for fellow teen Julian Hall, kick-starting a raft of changes from both sides.
Cole Campbell, 20, became the 13th US debutant of the post-World Cup international window.
Canada pushed forward, and their best chance came in the 63rd minute.
Substitute Mathieu Choiniere whipped in a free kick that De Fougerolles smartly volleyed, but his shot was tipped onto the crossbar at point-blank range by Brian Schwake.
Minutes later, Nathan Saliba flashed a cross across the face of goal but nobody was there to gather, and Canada's chances began to dwindle as the game petered out.

item.title: Ronaldo says Portugal coach broke promises, apologises for walkout
item.description:
Cristiano Ronaldo on Tuesday accused Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of breaking his word about giving him game time in Nations League matches, but said he remained available for his country.
In a statement of nearly 2,000 words, the 41-year-old superstar apologised for walking out on the national team and said he would serve a suspension if necessary.
"I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team," Ronaldo said.
Jesus left the forward unused on the bench for a Nations League match against Norway. Before the next game with Denmark, he said Ronaldo would not start and in response the 41-year-old walked out of the national team camp.
"I owe an apology to my national team teammates for having left the camp," wrote Ronaldo.
"Despite the absolute breakdown of trust in the head coach's word... I shouldn't have done it. The responsibility is mine alone."
Ronaldo also apologised to Portugal supporters, but insisted he had been responding to the veteran coach's "broken word".
"I apologise to the Portuguese people once again, but a broken word has, for me, a defining impact," said Ronaldo.
"I felt that, from that moment on, my presence would only harm the group, and I did what I always said I would do if I didn't feel useful: I picked up my bags and left."
Ronaldo said Jesus, who was appointed after Portugal were knocked out of the World Cup Round of 16, had initially presented him with a plan for the international window which included starting the opening and final games at home, but not travelling for the matches in Norway and Denmark.
The Al-Nassr superstar rejected that proposal, saying it would set a poor example for the captain to remain in Portugal while his team-mates travelled.
Ahead of the Norway game, Ronaldo said Jesus unexpectedly asked if he was fit to play 30 minutes. He agreed and warmed up from half-time, but was not brought on.
"The head coach failed to keep his word to me," said Ronaldo, Portugal's most capped player and all-time top goalscorer.
Former Real Madrid and Manchester United forward Ronaldo said he spoke with Jesus after that and agreed with him that the coach would apologise in a news conference ahead of the Denmark game.
However Ronaldo said Jesus's subsequent press conference was completely different from what was agreed in their conversation, with an "aggressiveness" he had never previously experienced from the coach.
"It was the second time he failed to keep his word. I decided to leave the camp without waiting for any further broken promises," wrote Ronaldo.
The striker said he would serve any "suspension that is imposed" on him and accepted he should be punished for his actions.
"The consequence of this act of mine must be assessed and punished by the Portuguese Football Federation," he explained.
"I understand that the punishment should not have mitigating circumstances. I'm not just any player, I'm the team captain, and that is an aggravating factor."
Portugal won all four of their Nations League matches and qualified for the quarter-finals with two games to spare.

item.title: Spain fight back to beat Croatia, Kane adds to record for England
item.description:
Spain fought back against Croatia to win 2-1 in Split on Tuesday and remain perfect in Nations League Group A3 while Harry Kane continued his hot form as England beat the Czech Republic 3-0 to stay second.
The victory in Split preserved Spain's long unbeaten run and ensured they will finish in the top two in the four-team group and advance to the quarter-finals.
England stayed three points behind Spain with a home win and will advance to the last four if they do not lose their next game at home to Croatia by eight or more goals.
In their previous match, Croatia capitulated 7-0 to England up the Dalmatian coast at Rijeka. Because of a ban brought on by persistent fan racism, that crowd was made up of 6,000 children under the age of 14.
In a very different atmosphere, Croatia gave a spikier performance and took the lead after 17 minutes. Unai Simon dived to save a low drive from Igor Matanovic but only pushed the ball into the air. Ivan Perisic, a former teammate of Kane at Tottenham, nodded the ball home.
While Spain dominated first-half possession, Croatia created the most dangerous chances and Matanovic could have doubled the lead.
Spain's pressure told after 61 minutes, Dani Olmo collected a poor clearance and rolled the ball to substitute Mikel Merino who had space to pick his spot.
Perisic had earned a yellow card for an excited lunge soon after scoring. That turned into a costly sending off when he was booked again after 79 minutes for a push on Marc Cucurella.
With a minute of normal time left, Merino found space in the box to turn and drive home the winner.
"Another game in which it was my turn to score from the bench," Merino told TVE, adding: "I'll go out there with the best possible attitude even while frustrated about not being able to play more... but this team is a family and that always shows."
The win stretched Spain's unbeaten run to 42 games. The one blemish in that run for the European and World Champions was a penalty shootout loss to Portugal after the last Nations League final had ended in a draw.
"There are days like today when the streak can become complicated," said Merino.
England lost their opener at home to Spain, when Kane missed a penalty that would have salvaged a draw, but have since won three games. Their veteran striker scored once away to the Czechs and twice in Croatia.
On Tuesday, as he equalled the England appearance record held by goalkeeper Peter Shilton with a 125th cap, Kane stretched his national scoring record to 91 with another double.
"Perfect night for me personally and also for the team," Kane told ITV on the pitch. "An extremely proud evening."
England were presented with their opener after 27 minutes when Vladimir Coufal, perhaps imagining an attacker behind him, smashed an England cross into his own net.
Kane finished off a quick, clever England attack by wrong-footing the goalkeeper from close range after 40 minutes. He hit the crossbar early in the second half and then headed home a corner after 57 minutes.
"You saw some fantastic football from us tonight," said Kane.
"As a striker you're just licking your lips and waiting for your opportunities."
Kane received praise from team-mate Jude Bellingham.
"He's playing at a level where it's pretty unmatched, when you look across the world," said the Real Madrid star.
"He's scoring goals for fun, he's still dropping in deep and delivering those passes in behind and wide and contributing in so many areas of the pitch."
In League B, Ryan Christie coolly flicked the ball between his legs to score a 31st-minute opener for Scotland at home to Slovenia but Aljosa Matko and Danijel Sturm hit back after half time to give the visitors a 2-1 win.
Leaders Switzerland ensured they will finish in the top two after they beat North Macedonia 3-0 in Lucerne, Fabian Rieder gave the hosts a first-half lead and Johan Manzambi and Dan Ndoye added late goals.

item.title: Guardians of the cage
item.description:
It was a cold, crisp, snowy day in February 1966 when in a New York City studio, a masterpiece of a song, "It's a Man's Man's Man's World" was co-written by James Brown and Betty Jean Newsome.
James Brown, who was then at the absolute peak of his commercial popularity, performed this song in live shows for the rest of his musical career.
The song starts with "This is a man's world" and goes on to aggressively ascribe all the works of the modern civilization such as cars, trains, boats, and electric light solely to male efforts; however, as if to pour oil on troubled waters, the song ends with a casual claim that it all would mean "Nothin' without a woman or a girl."
Interestingly, while Brown globally popularized the phrase "This is a man's world" through his "biblically chauvinistic" track, Newsome later claimed to have written the lyrics based on her own observations of gender dynamics.
Do you see the irony? This historic anthem that was profoundly criticized for its extreme machismo was given its meaning by Newsome, a woman herself, who fought for decades so her name was not erased from its history.
Sixty years ago, a phrase became universal due to the lyrical genius of a woman; the same phrase is still being used by our male-dominated society whenever patriarchy demands our women to be put in their “rightful” position.
In 1990, Sylvia Walby defined patriarchy as “a system of social structures and practices in which men dominate, oppress, and exploit women.” In other words, patriarchy is a system that predominantly favours men.
Yet, are men the only ones to forge ahead with patriarchy? Has it ever crossed your mind how women themselves, wearing the invisible cloak of patriarchy, have been perpetuating the faults of the system in the name of tradition all this time?
One bewildering characteristic of patriarchy is that it pits women against women. Each time a mother, a female teacher, a mother-in-law, a female friend, points the policing fingers at the woman next to her for not yielding to the system, the chain of patriarchy moves forward.
It is a common experience of girls growing up in Bangladesh to face judgement from women. The mechanism of patriarchy is so deeply rooted into our society that many women preach oppression instead of being a part of the sisterhood.
Remember the legendary cartoon Meena ? In this timeless children’s show, Meena’s mother and grandmother, clearly biased towards her brother Raju, would often discriminate between the siblings. Sadly, most girls born and growing up with brothers in Bangladeshi households are no stranger to this discrimination.
Unfortunately, the very first whip of patriarchy almost always comes from the mothers, who are often found policing their daughters’ bodies and behaviours so that the daughters conform to the entrenched norms of this patriarchal society.
Mothers often teach their daughters to adjust, to endure, to follow the rules, while their sons grow up knowing the world will negotiate the rules for them.
One survey showed that 93% families in Bangladesh see their sons as a blessing, while 96% see their daughters as a “problem” to the family and the country. The discrimination is reflected in dietary portions, permission to play outside, and the freedom to make friends.
This motherly discrimination is topped with the unwanted surveillance of the “aunty society.” The women from the neighbourhood or the mothers waiting outside schools and coaching centres almost invariably engage in tracking down girls for having male friends, talking or laughing too loud, dressing up, or wearing light makeup. These small acts of freedom often end up becoming the gravest of sins.
For many girls, even classrooms become a place for moral policing. Female teachers, who should be providing a safe outlet for the students, justify their humiliating remarks as “protection.” Moreover, in many co-ed institutions, female teachers sometimes show unfair preferences towards male students.
Among peers, women frequently face criticism disguised as opinions from other women, based on their life choices, work positions, or clothing.
Women who conform to societal expectations often feel superior and disdain women who choose to live lives that don’t align with those beliefs. Conformity thus turns into a currency for winning in life for women embodying patriarchy.
This submission to patriarchy continues as a mother-in-law’s abuse of her daughter-in-law activates the cycle of unjust treatment and passes it down from one generation to the next. As the mother of the groom, her actions of looking down on the bride's family and demanding dowry eventually turn into violence against the daughter-in-law.
And when the violent treatment compels the daughter-in-law to return to her parents’ house, it is often her mother who sends her back to her in-law’s house in the name of family honor. To these mothers, a dead daughter is far better than a divorced daughter.
So, should we consider these women culpable for the continuity of patriarchy? Before answering this question, we should ask a more important one: Why do women partake in this vile practice?
Denied direct power, as argued by author and academic Deniz Kandiyoti, many women learn to negotiate security by adapting to the system’s rules rather than resisting. Women submit to patriarchy as a survival mechanism and to gain authority over other women.
However, the consequences of this chain of patriarchy teach women to be each other’s judges instead of allies. It pierces through the sisterhood and hides structural patriarchy behind a facade of women blaming each other. Meanwhile, the system itself is perpetuated through whoever is closest to it.
To break through the shackles of patriarchy, women need to recognize the contradictions that make them the silent flag-bearers. Decoding the patterns can easily turn the contention into cohesion. This is why, when sisterhood refuses to become patriarchy’s ally, it motivates women to heal and grow together.
Nadia Afroze Disha is a lecturer at Brac Business School, Brac University. Purnasha Aurora is a student of Economics at Brac University.

item.title: WHO says no obesity drugs, surgery for under-10s
item.description:
Medicine and surgery are not the answer for overweight children, the World Health Organization said Wednesday.
Releasing its first guidelines addressing the sharp rise in obesity among children and adolescents, the WHO instead strongly recommended structured diets, physical activity and behavior changes.
“WHO does not recommend pharmacological treatment, bariatric surgery (surgery that changes the stomach or digestive tract) or weight-loss devices for children aged 0-9 years,” it said.
“For adolescents aged 10-19 years, treatment with approved medicines may be considered only when a supervised multimodal lifestyle program has not achieved the desired results.
“Bariatric surgery may be considered under strict conditions for adolescents with severe obesity.”
The recommendations for those aged 19 and under contrast with the UN health agency’s guidelines for adult obesity issued in December 2025, following the surge in popularity of a new generation of appetite-suppressing drugs called GLP-1 agonists -- which includes blockbuster brands Ozempic and Mounjaro.
The WHO said the range of weight-loss and diabetes drugs could be used for tackling obesity -- in adults.
In 2024, some 70 million children aged five to nine were obese, as were 100 million adolescents aged 10 to 19 worldwide, according to the WHO.
Among 5- to 19-year-olds, the prevalence of obesity has surged globally, rising from two percent in 1990 to eight percent in 2024.
“The rise of obesity is observed everywhere in all regions,” said Luz Maria De Regil, director of the WHO’s nutrition and food safety department.
“It’s growing in low- and middle-income countries,” while some high-income countries are starting to stop the rise of obesity, without yet making reductions.
“The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change,” she said.
The recommendations also stressed the importance of addressing mental health alongside obesity.
Anxiety, depression and low self-esteem can contribute to unhealthy eating, physical inactivity and social withdrawal, the WHO said.
Children and adolescents living with obesity may experience stigma and bullying, the UN health agency added.
Maria Nieves Garcia Casal, a scientist in the WHO’s nutrition and food safety department, told reporters that bariatric surgery may be considered during adolescence for cases of severe obesity accompanied by complications such as type 2 diabetes or hypertension -- if diet and lifestyle changes have failed.

item.title: Tennessee could still execute Christa Pike as experts warn of ‘uncharted territory’
item.description:
Tennessee officials could still choose to execute Christa Pike even after she survived the first two doses of a lethal injection drug last week, legal experts say.
Pike, 50, received two typically lethal doses of pentobarbital during a botched execution attempt in Nashville on September 30.
Her legal team revealed she was conscious and “speaking” six days after being rushed to hospital.
That would make her the first person to survive the administration of lethal injection drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike was sentenced to death for the murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in 1996, a crime committed when she was 18 years old.
In the aftermath of the execution attempt, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a third-party review of what went wrong.
Paul Lucas, an associate professor at East Carolina University, said the review would likely determine “what happens next.”
“If the investigation identifies problems with how the protocol was implemented, the state may focus on correcting those procedures,” he said.
“If officials followed the protocol as written and the execution nevertheless failed, that could raise more fundamental questions about the protocol itself.
“Either way, I would expect the circumstances surrounding Ms Pike’s failed execution to receive significant scrutiny before Tennessee resumes executions.”
While it remains unclear what exactly went wrong during the execution, experts have speculated the drug entered the tissue in Pike’s arm instead of entering her bloodstream.
Pike complained of her arm feeling like it was “about to burst open,” according to an emergency court filing after the attempt.
Her legal team has alleged at least seven syringes were used during attempts to establish an IV line, with at least one being “bent in a 90-degree angle.”
They had previously raised concerns about Pike’s health, including conditions which made lethal injection a riskier procedure.
“Upon arrival [to hospital] both of her arms were swollen, burned and blistered,”
court documents said.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was … entering Ms Pike’s body.”
Tennessee has paused all executions for the rest of the year, and the head of its Department of Corrections has resigned.
Dr Lucas said he was “hesitant” to predict what the state would do next.
“There are still too many unresolved questions, beginning with Ms Pike’s medical condition and the findings of the independent review,” he said.
“If the state does seek another execution, I would expect substantial litigation concerning whether another attempt can be carried out constitutionally given what occurred during the first one.”
The long-term ramifications, he added, could extend “beyond Tennessee.”
“A failed execution of this magnitude provides courts, policymakers, and other states with a real-world example through which to evaluate [lethal injection procedures],” he said.
“At a time when public support for capital punishment has generally declined from its historical highs, an event like this may also intensify the [debate about] how the death penalty is administered.
“Legally … changes in public attitudes do not by themselves determine a particular execution method is unconstitutional.”
The Death Penalty Information Center’s executive director Robin Maher said a second attempt was “uncharted territory.”
“The US Supreme Court has not decided whether a second execution attempt would violate the Constitution since 1947,” she told USA Today.
“These are questions that have never needed to be asked before and no-one knows the answers.”
Pike’s recovery was “medically unprecedented,” according to a statement released by her attorneys.
“We continue to ask the Governor of Tennessee to commute Christa Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole,” they said.
If Tennessee did decide to attempt another execution, it would not be the first time.
In May, death row inmate Tony Carruthers’ execution was called off after medical personnel could not establish an intravenous [IV] line after more than an hour of trying.
His lawyers challenged the qualifications of the doctor tasked with establishing IV access, Dr Mark Walton Fowler.
In an October deposition, Dr Fowler said he had no current hospital privileges and had last placed a central line more than a decade ago.
Dr Fowler said in an August interview with Fox News he would be overseeing Pike’s execution, something later confirmed by the Death Penalty Information Center.
Carruthers, who was sentenced to death for a 1994 triple murder, was granted a one-year reprieve following the attempt.
Giving Pike life in prison seemed to be “the most obvious recourse”, Fordham Law School professor Deborah Denno told CNN.
“Maybe [that’s] a decision that would go up to the United States Supreme Court,” she said.
“We certainly have seen a couple of instances of an inmate who has survived to be executed finally again.
“But that’s highly problematic, and I can’t imagine that happening in this kind of situation.
“Even if somebody is for the death penalty and thinks certain people deserve it, what happened to Christa Pike was never supposed to take place.”
Pike’s legal team has asked a court to order Tennessee officials to preserve evidence relating to the failed execution.
A hearing has been scheduled for 11am on October 7, local time.
Pike’s legal team was expected to hold another press conference sometime that afternoon.

item.title: Yemen’s Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi airports as conflict deepens
item.description:
The Houthis claimed a flurry of attacks on Saudi targets on Wednesday including firing a ballistic missile at Riyadh airport, as the group battles for territory in Yemen against government forces supported by the kingdom.
The Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen, captured swathes of coastal land from Yemen’s pro-government forces last month after the country’s civil war reignited in July.
The internationally recognized government this week declared a counter-offensive and claims to have uprooted Houthi fighters from strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
But the Iran-backed Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
“Our armed forces have just targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate, by God’s grace, and led to a disruption of air traffic,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Wednesday in a post on X.
The Saudi-led military coalition that backs Yemen’s government said the missile was intercepted.
In a separate post the Houthis also said they targeted military supplies at a camp area near the airport in the Yemeni city of Aden, the interim capital for the government.
The Yemeni government’s Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport.
Saree earlier said drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia’s Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait and had “hit their targets accurately.”
It is the second time this week that the Houthis claimed to have attacked the main airport in the Saudi capital.
It is facing frequent temporary closures of its airspace, according to tracking website Flightradar24, but Saudi authorities have not publicly acknowledged the closures or confirmed any strikes targeting the facility.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has been fighting the Houthis since 2015, and is now trying to roll back the group’s latest advance.
On Monday, the coalition said it was providing air support for the counter-offensive launched by the Yemeni government forces.
After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen’s civil war re-erupted in July. Last month the Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea in the country’s deadliest fighting in years.
The renewed violence has also deepened the wider Middle East war, which has roiled world energy markets and snarled shipping routes in the region.
Yemen’s government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory -- home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
On Tuesday sources on both sides told AFP that fighting across the country had killed more than 270 government troops and Houthi fighters over the past day alone.
The Yemen conflict has also caused a dire humanitarian crisis that left most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.
More than 184,000 people have been displaced by the latest fighting, according to the United Nations.
Mohammed, a 33-year-old charity worker who fled from Mocha to Aden, told AFP on Tuesday that “people there are terrified.”
“Life in Mocha has come to a complete standstill -- there is no movement at all. The city has become a war zone,” he said.

item.title: Bestselling British author Jeffrey Archer dies at 86
item.description:
Archer, who sold more than 300 million books during a five-decade writing career, died “suddenly and peacefully at home” on Monday between writing sessions, according to his publisher HarperCollins.
Known for bestsellers including Kane and Abel and the Clifton Chronicles , Archer frequently drew on his hometown of Wellington, Somerset, in his fiction.
Archer was born in north London in 1940 and moved with his family to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset. In 1969, he was elected as the Conservative MP for Louth in Lincolnshire and served in Parliament for five years before becoming deputy chairman of the Conservative Party.
He entered the House of Lords in 1992 but was sentenced to four years in prison in 2001 after being convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice.
The conviction followed a libel case Archer brought against the Daily Star after the newspaper alleged that he had slept with a sex worker. Archer had been awarded £500,000 in damages, but the court later found that he had lied during the case, arranged a false alibi, and produced fake diary entries.
He was released in 2003 and remained a member of the House of Lords until retiring in 2024.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as “devastating news,” saying he remained “very much loved by the Conservative family.”
Former prime minister John Major said Archer had lived “one of the most remarkable lives of our age” and would be “much missed – and long remembered.”
Archer's final novel, Adam and Eve , was released on Tuesday.
Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth, who spent time with Archer on Sunday, said the author had been in good spirits while promoting the book in London.
“He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience,” Brandreth said.
Former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as “a remarkable man who did everything at full bore,” while former ministers Sajid Javid and Jeremy Hunt also paid tribute to him.
Michael Grade, who produced the television adaptation of Kane and Abel , described Archer as a “consummate storyteller” both in life and in his writing.
“He loved politics more than anything,” Grade said, adding that Archer's political ambitions were ultimately ended by the mistakes in his life.
Archer returned to his former school in Wellington last week to promote Adam and Eve . He had been due to appear at the Cheltenham Literature Festival on Saturday to discuss the novel.
Archer and his wife Mary celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said.

item.title: Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ tops Billboard global charts
item.description:
Taylor Swift has debuted at No 1 on both of Billboard’s global song charts with “Patient Zero,” adding another milestone to her chart record.
The song tops the Billboard Global 200 and Billboard Global Excl US charts for the week dated October 10, 2026.
The achievement gives Swift her eighth No 1 on the Global 200, tying her with BTS for the most chart-toppers since the chart was launched in 2020.
“Patient Zero” is Swift’s fifth No 1 on the Global Excl. US chart, moving her ahead of Bad Bunny and Ariana Grande among solo artists. BTS leads all acts with eight No 1s.
The song is one of four new tracks included on the deluxe edition of Swift’s 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl , titled The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore .
According to Luminate data cited by Billboard, “Patient Zero” recorded 70.7 million streams and sold 80,000 copies worldwide during the September 25 to October 1 tracking period.
Its music video, directed by Swift and starring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell, premiered during the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards on September 27.
The other three new tracks also made strong debuts on the Global 200. “Cleveland!” entered at No 2, “Babylon” at No 3 and “Pink Clouding” at No 5.
The results bring Swift’s total Global 200 top-10 entries to 47, surpassing Drake’s previous record of 45.
Meanwhile, “The Fate of Ophelia,” another track from The Life of a Showgirl , climbed to No 8 on the Global 200 after spending seven weeks at No 1. It also reached No 10 on the Global Excl. US chart.
All four new tracks entered the Global Excl. US top 10, with “Patient Zero” at No 1, “Cleveland!” at No 6, “Pink Clouding” at No 7 and “Babylon” at No 8.
Swift now has 34 top-10 entries on the Global Excl. US chart, extending her lead over Bad Bunny, who has 24.
The chart success comes after The Life of a Showgirl returned to No 1 on the Billboard 200 for a 13th non-consecutive week following the release of The Encore edition.
Billboard’s Global 200 and Global Excl. US charts rank songs based on streaming and download sales across more than 200 territories. The Global 200 includes US activity, while the Global Excl. US chart measures activity outside the country, with data compiled by Luminate.

item.title: Wahaj Ali spotted in Dhaka with Nusraat Faria
item.description:
Wahaj visited Bangladesh to attend the closing program of Emira: The Wedding Chapter , a two-day wedding and lifestyle exhibition held at the United Convention Centre in Dhaka on October 2 and 3.
The actor had announced his visit in a video message, saying he was looking forward to meeting his Bangladeshi fans. Organizers described him as a personal guest at the event.
During the program, Wahaj and Faria appeared together at a fashion presentation. Faria later shared photographs of the two actors on Facebook, saying she had walked in a Jamdani-inspired outfit representing Bangladesh’s heritage.
The photographs quickly circulated on social media, drawing attention from fans of both actors.
Wahaj is particularly popular among Bangladeshi audiences for his portrayal of Murtasim Khan in Tere Bin , which premiered in 2022 and starred him opposite Yumna Zaidi. The drama gained a large following across South Asia.
Wahaj began his television career in 2015 with Ishq Ibadat . He later appeared in dramas including Dil Nawaz , Fitoor and Ishq Jalebi .
He also portrayed Bangladeshi freedom fighter Shafi Imam Rumi in the 2021 historical drama Jo Bichar Gaye .
His performance as Murtasim Khan in Tere Bin brought him wider recognition across South Asia.
Faria, meanwhile, continues to work in Bangladeshi cinema and television. While her appearance with Wahaj has prompted fan speculation about a possible collaboration, no such project has been officially announced.

item.title: Nobel Peace Prize haunted by the ‘specter’ of Trump
item.description:
Donald Trump’s chances of winning the Nobel Peace Prize are seen as minimal, but his “specter” will cast its shadow over Friday’s announcement of the winner in Oslo, experts say.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee knows it will be under close scrutiny: Since his return to the White House in January 2025, the billionaire Republican has campaigned intensively for the prize and hasn’t hidden his disappointment at not winning it yet.
The chances of him getting the nod are however undermined by his war against Iran, his territorial ambitions -- sometimes at the expense of allies, as in Greenland -- and his attacks on international cooperation institutions and the media.
Even though he has not been lobbying as openly for the Nobel in recent weeks, Trump remains on everyone’s minds, with strong chances that the committee’s pick will, regardless of who they choose, be interpreted as direct or indirect criticism of the US president.
Trump is “the specter in the room,” said the head of the Peace Research Institute in Oslo (Prio), Haakon Gjerlow.
He said the Nobel committee must be asking itself: “Is there any potential for this prize to create harm rather than good in awarding it?” given the reactions that could emerge from the White House.
The Nobel Institute says it is unfazed.
“There’s always a lot of lobbying, and ultimately perhaps also attempts to exert pressure on the committee. So in one sense we’re very used to that,” the secretary of the committee, Kristian Berg Harpviken, told AFP.
“It’s not something we don’t discuss. Of course we have to discuss it, but it’s not like that influences the discussions in the room and decisions that come out,” he insisted.
Last year, the prestigious prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, a choice generally considered palatable to Trump.
Machado even gave him her Nobel gold medal, judging he deserved it after the capture of President Nicolas Maduro -- though she failed to obtain his political backing in exchange.
Those events could prompt the committee to this year choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, such as an individual or organization working to protect children or humanitarian efforts.
That could include the Save the Children charity and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of kids illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories -- a cause close to the heart of Trump’s wife Melania.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, could also be a potential laureate.
But the committee may also choose a laureate that could rub Trump the wrong way.
That could include the UN special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories Francesca Albanese, Pope Leo XIV, press freedoms with an award to the Committee to Protect Journalists, or international justice bodies such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
“We live in an age of predators. We have Trump, Putin, Netanyahu,” said Nobel historian Asle Sveen.
“They don’t want to have an international order. They want to have big powers with spheres of influence. And this court stands in the way,” he said, referring to the ICC.
A total of 287 individuals and organizations have been nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize, though the names on the list are kept secret for 50 years.
But peace remains elusive in many parts of the world: 65 armed conflicts involving at least one state actor were registered in 2025, the highest number since 1946, according to PRIO.
“At an overall level, it is clear that the world is not developing in the right direction,” said Harpviken.
“At the same time ... there is no lack of good initiatives. There is no lack of organizations or individuals who do good work,” he said.
“A peace prize may make more sense than ever.”

item.title: Forced out, assaulted, unpaid: Teachers remain under pressure
item.description:
A university vice-chancellor was allegedly forced to sign a resignation letter inside his office. A college principal was prevented from entering his institution. Teachers were pushed and assaulted amid demands for their removal.
More than two years after forced resignations and attacks on teachers emerged as a major concern across educational institutions, fresh incidents suggest the problem is far from over, despite repeated government directives intended to protect affected teachers and restore their jobs and salaries.
The Alliance of Deprived Institution Heads and Teachers estimates that around 4,500 teachers and heads of institutions have been affected since 2024.
It claims at least eight teachers died following physical or psychological trauma, more than 500 were injured or fell ill, and over 1,000 are still not receiving salaries or allowances.
The figures could not be independently verified.
The latest incident occurred at Rajshahi Medical University on Tuesday, when Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Md Jawadul Haque was allegedly forced to sign a resignation letter after a group entered his office while he was attending a virtual meeting with Health Ministry officials.
His personal secretary and section officer Nazmul Hossain was allegedly assaulted when he intervened and was also forced to sign a resignation letter.
Nazmul later filed a case with Rajpara Police Station. Police arrested Abdus Salam, 56, in connection with the incident.
Police initially said Salam’s political affiliation had not been confirmed.
Rajpara Thana BNP President Mizanur Rahman, however, told media that Salam was a vice-president of the thana BNP unit and had been present during the incident.
The RMU incident came less than two weeks after tensions at Mohammadpur Central College, where teachers alleged that students and outsiders obstructed Principal Lt Col (retd) Md Shahidul Hasan and harassed teachers.
On September 24, some students and outsiders allegedly locked the administrative building gate and demanded the principal’s removal amid tensions surrounding a Class XI orientation program.
Bangla lecturer Shawon Ahmed Kabir was allegedly pushed while trying to calm the situation, while teacher representative Dr Mohammad Shamsul Alam was also allegedly assaulted.
Teachers later submitted a written complaint seeking action, and the college governing body assured them that the allegations would be investigated.
Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal subsequently expelled two members over allegations linked to the incident.
Teacher representatives say such incidents form part of a much broader problem dating back to the political upheaval of 2024.
Alliance convener Anwarul Islam Talukder said more than 1,000 affected teachers were still not receiving salaries or allowances, while many had been unable to return to their institutions for more than a year.
“We have repeatedly approached the Education Ministry and the Secondary and Higher Education Division, but there has been little progress,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
The government has issued a series of directives since reports of forced resignations began emerging.
The Education Ministry said in September 2024 that forcing teachers to resign was unacceptable.
Further instructions followed concerning salaries and allowances, reinstatement and action against institutions that failed to comply.
Teacher representatives, however, say implementation remains incomplete.
Anwarul Islam, principal of Suapur Nannar School and College in Dhamrai, said he was among those forced from office after August 2024.
He alleged that a group of teachers and students accused him of irregularities on August 11 and demanded his resignation.
The following day, he said, around 15 people went to his Mirpur residence and forced him to sign a resignation letter.
Former Dhaka City College principal and alliance president Md Bedar Uddin Ahmed said the organization had repeatedly submitted complaints and memorandums to government offices.
“Despite government directives, many teachers are still unable to return to their workplaces,” he said.
Teachers from other institutions, including Viqarunnisa Noon School and College, have also previously alleged that they were forced to resign following the events of August 2024.
Acting principal Keka Roy and assistant professor Dr Farhana Khanam were among those who made such allegations.
The issue is now set to receive international scrutiny.
UN Special Rapporteur on the right to education Farida Shaheed is scheduled to visit Bangladesh from November 23 to December 4, according to information provided by the teachers’ alliance and reported by media.
The group says she will examine allegations involving teachers and students who faced mob attacks at educational institutions after August 5, 2024, with the Unesco Dhaka office assisting during the visit.
The alliance said affected teachers have submitted complaints and supporting materials for the process, including information on their employment status, cases, photographs, videos and audio recordings.
The exact number of complaints submitted has not been established.
Educationist Rasheda K Chowdhury said attacks and harassment of teachers, alongside disputes over salaries, allowances and professional dignity, reflected a broader crisis of confidence in the education system.
“If we want quality education, we need quality teachers,” she said, stressing the importance of both investment in and respect for the profession.
Prof Mohammad Mujibur Rahman of Dhaka University’s Institute of Education and Research said allegations against teachers should be investigated through due process, with teachers given an opportunity to respond before decisions are taken.
“Firstly, teachers need to act independently. Again, our perspective has yet to evolve. As a nation, we still fail to recognize the importance of education and those who teach,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
Educationists stressed that complaints against teachers or disputes over institutional decisions should not be ignored.
Allegations of misconduct or irregularities should be investigated and, where substantiated, acted upon.
But they said those processes should take place through established institutional and legal procedures, rather than physical intimidation, humiliation or forcing teachers to sign resignation letters.

item.title: 17-year-old Rakibul abducted for ransom, killed by friend
item.description:
Seventeen-year-old Md Rakibul Islam came to Dhaka after his HSC exams, hoping to prepare for university admission, but was allegedly abducted for ransom and later killed, police said.
Rakib was staying at a mess in East Shewrapara and attending a coaching centre in Farmgate. On September 16, he was called outside through a WhatsApp call but never returned.
According to police, Rakib became acquainted online with Abdullah Al Mamun alias Mamun Sarker, 24, shortly after arriving in Dhaka. Mamun allegedly called him to the area in front of Shewrapara Metro Rail Station on September 16 and took him to his home in Sukrabad.
Police said Mamun held Rakib hostage and demanded Tk15 lakh from his family. During a struggle, he allegedly twisted Rakib’s neck, causing his death.
Mamun then placed the body in a carton, sealed it with Scotch tape and took it by autorickshaw to Gabtoli bus terminal. He later travelled to Dimla in Nilphamari and buried the carton containing Rakib’s body in a pit in a betel nut orchard in front of his home on September 17, police said. DMP Crime Prevention (North) Joint Commissioner Md Mahidul Islam disclosed the details at a press briefing at the DMP Media Centre on Wednesday.
Police said the family paid Tk4 lakh through four bKash and three Nagad numbers after receiving ransom demands and threats to kill Rakib.
Rakib’s elder brother, Johurul Islam Jibon, initially filed a general diary with Kafrul Police Station and later filed a case over the abduction and ransom demand.
Mahidul said police traced Mamun as the user of two WhatsApp numbers used to demand the ransom. He was arrested from the Sukrabad bus stand area in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar on October 5.
During interrogation, Mamun reportedly confessed to taking Rakib to his home to collect the ransom and said Rakib died when he twisted his neck during a struggle.
Police recovered Rakib’s body from the spot indicated by Mamun in Dimla on Tuesday with the assistance of local police. His elder brother later identified the body.
The body was sent to Nilphamari Modern Sadar Hospital for autopsy.
Police also recovered Tk50,000 in cash, allegedly from the ransom money, from Mamun.
Mahidul said the investigation is underway to determine whether anyone else was involved and to examine the ransom transactions and other aspects of the case.

item.title: Ansar-VDP begins advance security measures for Durga Puja
item.description:
The Bangladesh Ansar and Village Defense Party (VDP) has begun advance security measures across the country to ensure the upcoming Sharodiya Durga Puja is celebrated safely and peacefully.
As part of the preparations, Ansar-VDP members are visiting idol-making sites, puja mandaps and temples, according to a press release issued on Wednesday.
The release said Ansar-VDP members at the field level are exchanging views with leaders of puja celebration committees, temple authorities and people involved in making idols.
The discussions cover idol security, the law and order situation during the puja, and the duties and responsibilities of puja celebration committees and Ansar-VDP members.
The activities are being carried out at district and upazila levels under the directive of Major General Abdul Motaleb Sajjad Mahmud, director general of the Bangladesh Ansar and Village Defense Party.
Allowance-receiving (stipendiary) Ansar-VDP members are working in the field under the supervision of upazila Ansar-VDP officers and instructors.
During the visits, those concerned are being advised to remain vigilant about the security of puja mandaps, entry and exit management, lighting arrangements and fire safety.
Emphasis is also being placed on coordination with local administration and law enforcement agencies to avoid any undesirable situation.
In addition, puja celebration committees have been requested to arrange accommodation and necessary facilities for Ansar members who will be on duty during the puja.
They have also been asked to cooperate in maintaining overall security and discipline at puja mandaps and in taking swift, coordinated action during emergencies.
The release further stated that Ansar-VDP members are being kept ready to perform duties at various puja mandaps across the country to ensure public safety and maintain law and order during the Sharodiya Durga Puja.
Through coordination with the local administration, law enforcement agencies and puja celebration committees, the advance preparations and field-level activities will continue to ensure a safe and peaceful puja.

item.title: Heading to Bangladesh? Dengue vaccine now an option in Australia
item.description:
As Bangladesh grapples with widespread dengue, the availability of a dengue vaccine in Australia has brought a new preventive option for Bangladeshi expatriates worried about travelling home with their families.
Qdenga, a vaccine designed to protect against dengue disease, has become available in Australia following approval by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), with the Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (ATAGI) issuing clinical advice on its use in September.
The development is particularly significant for Bangladeshis living in Australia, many of whom regularly travel home with their children and other family members and have become increasingly concerned about dengue infections and deaths in Bangladesh.
Qdenga is approved in Australia for people aged four years and above.
However, health authorities do not recommend that every traveller automatically receive it.
ATAGI particularly recommends Qdenga for eligible people who have previously had dengue and are at risk of future exposure.
For people aged four and above who have never had dengue and are undertaking short-term travel, vaccination can be considered following an individual risk-benefit assessment.
For Bangladeshi families in Australia, that means the vaccine offers another option to discuss with their doctors before travelling home.
Mohammad Irfan Khan, a resident of Lakemba in Sydney, is planning to take his children to Bangladesh during an upcoming holiday.
He said reports about the dengue situation in Bangladesh, particularly infections and deaths among children, had been a source of anxiety.
With Qdenga now available, he plans to consult a doctor about whether his children should be vaccinated before the trip.
Another expatriate, Syed Ashraf Ahmed, said dengue was a growing concern among Bangladeshis living abroad as they frequently heard about relatives, friends and acquaintances becoming seriously ill back home.
The availability of vaccination before travelling to Bangladesh, he said, offered some reassurance to expatriate families.
Qdenga is a live-attenuated vaccine targeting all four dengue virus serotypes.
The vaccine is administered in two 0.5ml doses. Under Australian guidance, the doses are given three months apart, and completing the two-dose course is important for maximising protection.
There is currently insufficient evidence to support routine booster doses.
Dengue is transmitted primarily by infected Aedes mosquitoes.
Symptoms can include sudden fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, fatigue and rash. While many infections are mild, severe dengue can become life-threatening.
Previous infection is particularly relevant because subsequent infection with another dengue serotype can, in some circumstances, carry a greater risk of severe disease.
Almost all dengue cases notified in Australia are acquired overseas, highlighting the risk faced by international travellers visiting countries where transmission is common.
Australia itself recorded 2,381 dengue notifications in 2024 and 1,863 in 2025, according to figures cited in the source material.
Health professionals stress, however, that vaccination does not replace protection against mosquito bites.
Travellers to Bangladesh and other dengue-affected destinations should continue using mosquito repellent, wearing protective clothing and taking other precautions to minimise exposure.
For Bangladeshi expatriates preparing to visit home, Qdenga therefore does not remove the dengue risk.
But it does provide something newly available in Australia: an additional preventive option that families can discuss with their doctors before travelling.

item.title: Policy dialogue calls for rights-based digital governance in Bangladesh
item.description:
A policy dialogue in Dhaka has called for stronger protection of privacy, freedom of expression and digital safety, along with greater institutional accountability, as Bangladesh’s use of technology continues to expand.
The “Policy Dialogue on Rights-Respecting Digital Governance in Bangladesh” brought together parliamentarians, policymakers, civil society representatives, journalists and young people to discuss building a safer, more inclusive and rights-based digital governance system.
The dialogue was organised by SERAC-Bangladesh, with support from DDI South Asia and Accountability Lab.
MP Anisur Rahaman of Madaripur-3, MP Salah Uddin of Gazipur-4 and reserved women’s seat MP Sherin Sultana attended the event, along with representatives from civil society, the media and youth groups.
The programme began with welcome remarks by Mizanur Rahman Akanda, project manager of SERAC-Bangladesh.
S M Shaikat, executive director of SERAC-Bangladesh, delivered the keynote presentation, focusing on protecting citizens, ensuring youth participation and strengthening institutional accountability to build a safe and rights-respecting digital Bangladesh.
The roundtable discussion was moderated by Md Salim Miah, director (programme) of SERAC-Bangladesh.
Freedom of expression was a key focus of the discussion.
Participants said the right to express opinions must be protected both online and offline, while stressing that exercising this right should not infringe on the rights, dignity, privacy or safety of others.
They called for a balanced approach to online expression, saying legitimate criticism and public debate should be protected, while threats, incitement to violence, fraud and other harmful activities should be addressed through clear, necessary and proportionate legal measures.
Participants also stressed the importance of accuracy and context in news and digital content, saying incomplete or one-sided reporting can mislead the public and distort perceptions of events.
Data privacy was another major concern at the dialogue.
Participants, including MPs, discussed the difficulties citizens face in correcting or updating their personal information.
They highlighted a contrast between the difficulties people often experience in correcting or updating their National Identity (NID) information and concerns that sensitive personal data may be obtained by unauthorised individuals for relatively small amounts of money.
The discussion referred to reported payments ranging from Tk30 to Tk250 for access to personal information.
Participants said institutions collecting and processing personal data should collect only information necessary for specific purposes and restrict access based on official responsibilities.
They also called for transparent and auditable records of who accesses and uses personal data, clear accountability for handling such information and effective remedies for unlawful access or misuse.
The dialogue also highlighted growing digital risks for children and young people.
Participants identified online harassment, identity misuse, manipulated and AI-generated content, and unauthorised use of personal information as major concerns.
They called for confidential and accessible complaint mechanisms, timely remedies and appropriate psychosocial support for young people facing online harm.
Participants also stressed that young people should not be treated merely as beneficiaries of digital policies. Instead, they should have a meaningful role in developing laws and policies affecting their digital lives, with their experiences and perspectives reflected in decision-making.
They further called for greater coordination among laws and policies on cybersecurity, personal data protection and national data management, as well as clear and accessible mechanisms for citizens to seek remedies when their rights are violated.
The dialogue also stressed the need to consult young people, civil society, technology experts, legal professionals, journalists and affected communities before introducing new digital laws and policies.
Participants identified several priorities for improving digital governance, including clear definitions of digital offences, proportionate enforcement of laws, stronger institutional accountability for personal data, safer digital participation for children, young people and women, meaningful public consultation and stronger parliamentary oversight.
They said Bangladesh’s digital transformation must be accompanied by stronger safeguards for fundamental rights, privacy, safety, dignity and freedom of expression.
They emphasised that digital governance should evolve alongside technological development while remaining accountable, transparent, inclusive and respectful of citizens’ rights.

item.title: German tourist loses bag after leaving it with railway official in Natore
item.description:
An 18-year-old German tourist lost his bag containing a laptop, camera and other valuables at Natore Railway Station on Wednesday after leaving it with a railway official before going to an ATM.
The tourist, identified as Kirill, arrived at the station by train from Bogra at around 4pm and left the bag in the waiting room before heading out to withdraw cash.
Kirill said he left his belongings with a railway official wearing a vest, who assured him that he would look after the items while he was away.
When he returned after withdrawing money, neither the official nor his bag and belongings could be found, he said.
Kirill said he searched in and around the station but could not locate his belongings.
According to Kirill, the iCloud location of his laptop showed that it was in the Naogaon area at around 6:40pm on Wednesday. The location data has raised hopes that the missing belongings may be recovered.
Kirill subsequently contacted railway authorities and was referred to Natore Sadar Police Station. He remained there for an extended period awaiting assistance and was seen breaking down in tears.
Natore Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge Monsur Rahman said the matter primarily falls under the jurisdiction of railway police.
“However, as the victim is a foreign national, we are treating the matter with the utmost importance,” he said.
The OC said police had already identified the location of the missing devices and sent a team there.
“We hope to recover Kirill’s laptop, camera and other missing belongings soon,” he added.

item.title: PM: Religion, identity must not stand in way of citizens’ rights
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday pledged to build a Bangladesh where religion, race or identity will not stand in the way of anyone’s rights and opportunities, with equal rights and dignity for every citizen.
“We want to build a Bangladesh where religion, race or identity will not stand in the way of people’s rights and opportunities. Our goal is to ensure equal rights and dignity for every citizen of the country,” he said.
The prime minister made the remarks at a view-exchange meeting with representatives of the Hindu and Buddhist communities at his office at the Secretariat, said his Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin.
During the meeting, representatives of the Hindu community thanked the prime minister for extending the government holiday for Durga Puja, saying the decision has added to the festive joy of the Hindu community.
The representatives of the Hindu and Buddhist communities also raised various problems, needs and demands before the prime minister.
Tarique Rahman listened to their views and assured them that the government is sincerely working for the welfare of people from all communities.
“We will make our utmost efforts to do whatever is possible on behalf of the government. Your reasonable demands and problems will be considered with importance,” he said.
The Hindu community representatives invited the prime minister to visit different Durga Puja mandaps during five-day Durga Puja beginning on October 17.
Tarique Rahman extended greetings to members of the Hindu community on the occasion of Durga Puja and to members of the Buddhist community on the occasion of Kathin Chibar Dan.
He also wished peace, prosperity and welfare for all citizens of the country.
The representatives of the two communities, in turn, extended greetings to the prime minister on the occasion of their respective religious festivals.
Later, the prime minister handed over cheques – for Tk 5 crore to the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust for Durga Puja and Tk 3 crore to the Buddhist Religious Welfare Trust for the Buddhist religious festival.
The Hindu Religious Welfare Trust had sought Tk 4 crore for Durga Puja, while the prime minister approved Tk 5 crore as a special consideration.
Similarly, the Buddhist Religious Welfare Trust had sought Tk 2 crore for the Kathin Chibar Dan festival, but Tarique Rahman approved Tk 3 crore, also as a special consideration.
The government has also declared a three-day holiday from October 20 to 22 on the occasion of Durga Puja, allowing a five-day holiday as October 23 and 24 are weekend.
The allocated funds will be distributed among the beneficiaries through the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust and district administrations. The beneficiaries will be able to receive the money directly through their bank accounts.
Representatives of the Hindu and Buddhist communities thanked the prime minister for increasing the allocations and expressed their gratitude to the government.

item.title: Family planning campaign begins December 1 with ‘Two children’ slogan
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain has announced a nationwide family planning campaign from December 1 to encourage people to limit family size.
Speaking to reporters at his office on Wednesday, the minister said the month-long awareness campaign would be conducted under the slogan, “No more than 2 children, one is better.”
The campaign will include rallies, fairs and various awareness programs across the country. Essential family planning supplies will also be delivered to households, he said.
“We will not just talk about it. We will also supply all the necessary materials. Tablets, contraceptives, pads—whatever is needed for family planning will be delivered to households,” the minister said.
He said the director general of the Directorate General of Family Planning and other officials concerned had been working over the past few days to prepare an implementation plan for the campaign.
Various programs will be organized at the district level to encourage people to adopt family planning practices, he added.
The minister said government spending must follow specific rules and procedures, which often takes time. As a result, many planned activities could not be implemented in the past.
“Work has now started afresh, and visible progress will be seen from the beginning of next year,” he said.
Describing family planning as one of the weaker areas of the country’s health sector, Sakhawat said the sector had failed to make the expected progress.
He also said there were several challenges to reducing the country’s birth rate.

item.title: 22-day ban on ilish catching begins at midnight
item.description:
The government has imposed a ban on ilish catching, selling, transporting and hoarding for the next 22 days, from Wednesday midnight to protect mother Hilsa and ensure safe breeding. The restriction will remain effective from Thursday to October 29. The decision was taken at a meeting of the National Taskforce Committee on Hilsa Resource Development held at the conference room of the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock and the Ministry of Agriculture recently. According to the decision, transportation, storage, marketing, buying, selling and exchange of ilish will also remain prohibited across the country during the ban period. The government will provide Vulnerable Group Feeding (VGF) food assistance to fishermen who refrain from fishing during the period. Fishermen are starting to return from the deep sea to fish landing centres as the ban approaches. In Chandpur, a 22-day ban on fishing has begun in a 70-kilometre stretch of the Padma-Meghna rivers in Chandpur to ensure the safe breeding of ilish and protect the country's national fish resource. Ahead of the ban, many fishermen in Chandpur have already brought their boats and fishing nets ashore. While some are repairing their boats, others are busy mending damaged nets.
Meanwhile, district and upazila task forces have taken preparations to enforce the restriction. It was found that fishermen preparing for the 22-day fishing halt while visiting different fishing communities from Wednesday morning to noon.
The areas visited included Anandabazar in Tarpur Chandi Union of Sadar upazila, Tilabari on Jamuna Road, Ranagowal and Dokanghar areas of Puran Bazar, Ramdasdi and Baharia in Laxmipur Model Union, and the fishing village near Harina ferry terminal in Hanarchar Union. At Anandabazar, most fishermen were seen pulling their boats ashore, while some were repairing them. Similar scenes were observed at Baharia Bazar.
Fishermen in Ramdasdi were busy mending their nets while boat repair workers were seen working on several vessels near Harina ferry terminal.
Abul Kalam, 54, a fisherman from Anandabazar, said he had not caught much ilish in the river this season.
"I have already brought my boat ashore. I will put it back into the river after 22 days, depending on the availability of ilish," he said.
Khaleq Gazi, 52, a fisherman from Ramdasdi, said the government conducts the annual operation to protect mother ilish, but enforcement sometimes falls short because of inadequate planning.
"Patrolling should also be arranged in the canals connected to the Meghna so that unscrupulous fishermen cannot catch mother ilish," he said. Idris Ali, a fish trader from Baharia, said traders were ready to cooperate with the administration and police to ensure the safe spawning of ilish.
Veteran fish trader Sirajul Islam Sayed of Harina fish landing centre said the fishing ban should begin at the river's mouth near the sea before reaching the sanctuary areas, because many mother ilish are caught there and subsequently sent to markets. Chandpur Sadar Upazila Fisheries Officer Mirza Omar Faruk said several coordination meetings had already been held to ensure enforcement of the 22-day ban. "Awareness campaigns are being conducted in the Meghna coastal areas to warn fishermen against catching mother ilish," he said. Chandpur District Fisheries Officer Md Fakhrul Islam said district and upazila task forces would conduct regular drives in the sanctuary areas under Chandpur's river boundaries to protect ilish during the breeding season. "Anyone violating the law by entering the river for fishing will be brought under legal action," he added. He further said 41,000 registered fishermen who have been instructed to refrain from fishing during the ban have already received 25 kilograms of rice each as government assistance.

item.title: DU professor Jamal Uddin shown arrested in another anti-terrorism case after bail
item.description:
Professor AKM Jamal Uddin of Dhaka University’s Department of Sociology has been shown arrested in another anti-terrorism case after securing bail in a separate case.
Dhaka Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Jashita Islam passed the order on Wednesday following a petition by the investigating officer, said SI Rokonuzzaman of the prosecution department.
Police arrested Jamal Uddin on March 11 while he was taking part in a programme titled “Bangabandhu Peace March-2026” at Gulistan Zero Point in the capital.
He was later shown arrested in an anti-terrorism case filed with Paltan Model Police Station and sent to jail the same day. He recently secured bail from the High Court in that case.
On October 1, SI Md Nuruzzaman of Paltan Model Police Station sought an order to show Jamal Uddin arrested in another anti-terrorism case filed with the same police station.
The court fixed Wednesday for the hearing, and Jamal Uddin was brought before it from jail.
Public prosecutor Muhammad Shamsuddoha Sumon argued in favour of the police petition, while defence lawyer Md Khair Uddin Sikder opposed it.
After hearing both sides, the court reserved its order and later directed that Jamal Uddin be shown arrested in the case.
Advocate Md Khair Uddin Sikder said Jamal Uddin had secured bail from the High Court in an anti-terrorism case filed with Paltan Model Police Station. After the bail order was sent to the jail authorities, police sought to show him arrested in another case filed under the same law.
“He was shown arrested in the case today,” the lawyer said.
He also said Jamal Uddin is facing a case before the International Crimes Tribunal.
According to the case statement, members, financiers, advisers and instigators of the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League gathered in Gulistan, Baitul Mukarram and adjoining areas on May 18, 2025, allegedly to carry out acts of sabotage and destruction.
Police conducted a raid in front of Hotel Imperial, opposite the south gate of Baitul Mukarram, and detained several people. Around 140–150 unidentified people fled in different directions.
Police filed the anti-terrorism case with Paltan Model Police Station the same day.

item.title: Three arrested as adulterated, unapproved medicines made in Mohammadpur flat
item.description:
Adulterated and unapproved medicines, including children’s syrups, capsules and tablets, were being manufactured and stored for sale from a flat in Mohammadpur, Dhaka, where the Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police seized medicines and manufacturing equipment worth around Tk1 crore and arrested three members of the gang during a raid.
The DB is also searching for doctors who prescribed the unapproved medicines to patients. DB chief and Additional Commissioner Md Shafiqul Islam said legal action would be taken against doctors found to be involved.
He shared the information in response to journalists’ questions at a press conference on Wednesday at the DMP Media Center.
Md Shafiqul Islam said the DB conducted the raid on Tuesday based on intelligence information at a third-floor flat in a building on Block-C of Dhaka Uddyan Road under Mohammadpur Police Station.
The arrested are Abdullah Al-Mamun, 42, Md Saju, 33, and Md Sajib, 26.
A large quantity of adulterated medicines was recovered, including syrups, capsules, shampoos, face washes, hygiene washes, soaps, powders and tablets.
The seized items include 192 bottles of KIDZ Omega Liquid 100ml syrup, 100 boxes of LACTOFLEX Capsules, 30 Facy GLOW Face Wash, 150 Detox Plus Shampoo, 70 Pedia Vox Kid Syrup, 300 strips of Osearc-CD capsules, 5kg of Oriva Hapes white powder, 50 BIOKET Active Shampoo, 800 KIDICARE Syrup Plus 100ml, 70 ZERO DAN Shampoo, 40 KETCOR-Z Shampoo and 10 Nutramide Syrup.
Also recovered were 150 empty packets of INTA CLEAN HYGIENE WASH, 80 unpackaged bottles of Hygiene Wash, 300 empty packets of PERMIMITE Soap, 80 Spiruva (Spirulina) leaflets, 100 polythene covers for face wash, 300 unlabelled syrup bottles, 400 white plastic containers, 100 unlabelled white tablets and 500 empty green capsule shells.
The DB also seized 3 cylinders used in making the medicines, a fuel-filling machine, 2 capsule-filling machines, 10kg of fuel in polythene, 6 capsule-filling machine parts and 2 label-attaching stamps.
The DB chief said several syrups and liquid products for children were among the recovered items. He said the adulterated and unapproved medicines could pose a serious risk to children’s lives and health.
A case was filed at Mohammadpur Police Station under the Special Powers Act against the 3 arrested, accusing them of keeping adulterated medicines in their possession for sale.
Asked how ordinary people can identify adulterated medicines, Md Shafiqul Islam said it is extremely difficult to recognize them. However, he said they can in many cases be identified by closely examining the medicine’s packaging and the relevant company’s packaging.
He said some of the medicines found in the raid are not in circulation in the country and, according to preliminary information, were imported from a neighboring country. He also said the medicines were being prescribed to patients through certain doctors.
Asked how much medicine the gang had already supplied to the market, given that medicines worth about Tk1 crore were seized, the DB chief said the matter was under investigation.
Documents found during the raid are being reviewed, he said, adding that everyone involved would be brought under the law after the investigation.
Md Shafiqul Islam said the seized medicines included foreign products, and whether they were legally imported into the country was also being investigated.
The DB chief said some medicines for children were also found during the raid. Among them, he identified a syrup named Kidocare as counterfeit. Some medicines for children related to Kid Omega and Vitamin D3 were also seized.

item.title: ACI Beverages brings Singaporean coffee brand MacCoffee to Bangladesh
item.description:
ACI Beverages, a strategic unit under ACI Foods Limited, has officially launched MacCoffee in Bangladesh through a strategic collaboration with Empire International Sdn. Bhd. (a member of Food Empire Holdings Limited, Singapore) facilitated by Mitsui & Co. (Malaysia) SDN BHD.
The official launch ceremony took place at one of Shwapno’s flagship outlets in Banasree D Block on Wednesday, October 7.
The launch event was attended by senior officials from ACI, including Rezaul Islam, president, ACI Consumer Brands, and Zakir Ibne Hai, executive director & chief operating officer, ACI Food and Beverage.
Representatives from Empire International Sdn. BHD., including Pradeep Chauhan (director, Empire International SDN BHD) and Tan Boon Hua (general manager, Empire International SDN BHD), were also present, alongside Kenichiro Kawamoto, country chairperson of Mitsui & Co., (Asia Pacific) PTE LTD, Dhaka Branch.
The collaboration marks another significant milestone in ACI Beverages’ journey to build a diverse beverage portfolio in Bangladesh.
ACI Beverages began its journey in the beverage category with the distribution of Sunquick Fruit Concentrate and Fruit Drink products, followed by the launch of ACI Electrolyte Drinks, marking its entry into the beverage industry.
