Building on the growing portfolio and recognizing the significant potential of the hot beverage category in Bangladesh, ACI Beverages partnered with Empire International Sdn. Bhd. (Singapore) to bring MacCoffee to consumers across the country.
MacCoffee is a renowned and trusted coffee brand, loved by consumers across 60+ countries worldwide.
With its strong global reputation and commitment to delivering quality coffee experiences. MacCoffee brings a truly international coffee brand to the growing coffee lovers of Bangladesh.
The collaboration initially begins with the distribution of MacCoffee Original and MacCoffee Gold jars in Bangladesh. With the long-term vision of strengthening its local presence, the partnership also aims to commence local packaging of MacCoffee products, alongside introducing new and exciting products to the market.

item.title: BAT Bangladesh appoints Momshad Ali Khan as head of corporate & regulatory affairs
item.description:
BAT Bangladesh PLC. has appointed Momshad Ali Khan as its head of corporate & regulatory affairs, effective October 1, 2026.
Momshad brings more than two decades of experience across corporate affairs, government relations, regulatory strategy, stakeholder engagement and strategic communications.
Before joining BAT Bangladesh, he served as director, public affairs, communications and sustainability at Coca-Cola Bangladesh, where he was also a member of the Bangladesh Leadership Team.
Prior to that, he held the position of head of corporate and fiscal affairs at JT International Bangladesh.
Earlier in his career, Momshad spent more than a decade at Chevron Bangladesh, building extensive experience in the corporate affairs space.
Momshad holds an MBA from the University of Dhaka and an Executive MBA from American International University Bangladesh (AIUB).
Commenting on his appointment, Momshad Ali Khan said: “I am honoured to join an organization with a legacy of more than 116 years in this region. I look forward to working with the talented team to drive the company’s sustainable success, strengthen its role as a development partner to the nation, and navigate the evolving policy and regulatory landscape.”

item.title: Shama Obaed: Cox’s Bazar insecurity ‘cannot become the new normal’
item.description:
Seeking a genuine solution to the Rohingya crisis, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Wednesday warned that rising crime and insecurity affecting Cox’s Bazar host communities “cannot be allowed to become the new normal.”
She said the solution lies in Myanmar and that Bangladesh cannot sustain the crisis indefinitely.
The state minister urged the international community to move from statements of support to actionable and predictable assistance.
She addressed the National Policy Dissemination Program on “Uncertain Return: Rohingya Voices on Repatriation Barriers,” organized by the Department of Criminology and the Criminology Research Forum of the University of Dhaka, as chief guest at the Senate Bhaban, University of Dhaka.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam addresses the National Policy Dissemination Programme on ’Uncertain Return: Rohingya Voices on Repatriation Barriers’ at the Senate Bhaban, University of Dhaka, on Wednesday, October 7, 2026. Photo: UNB
In her speech as the chief guest, the state minister recalled the address of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the 81st UNGA and highlighted the five urgent priorities he set before the international community: from a credible roadmap for sustainable repatriation to an end to violence, justice, accountability and stronger action against transnational crimes.
She noted the formation of a National Strategy Formulation Committee to guide the Rohingyas’ safe and dignified return.
Referring to the study conducted by the Department of Criminology on the envisaged return of the forcibly displaced Myanmar nationals (FDMNs), she mentioned that the Rohingyas are not rejecting Myanmar as their home.
They are rejecting a return to the conditions that forced them to flee.
She identified recognition and identity, land and property, security, and trust with credible guarantees as the pillars of a credible roadmap, adding that “repatriation is an act of trust” and that the Rohingyas are “asking for rights, not charity.”
Earlier, the research team introduced the research, which had surveyed 816 Rohingya respondents across 17 camp sites in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar.
They had also conducted 72 in-depth interviews with stakeholders involved in the repatriation process.
The state minister also distributed prizes among winners of an "Essay Competition" organized by the Department of Criminology.

item.title: Mahdi Amin: Govt committed to workers’ rights, better working conditions
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Adviser on Labour and Employment Mahdi Amin has said the government is committed to protecting workers’ rights, creating jobs and ensuring better working conditions.
“Protecting workers’ rights and creating widespread employment opportunities are the government’s priorities,” he said.
He made the remarks during a courtesy meeting with a high-level delegation from the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC) and the International Organisation of Employers (IOE) at the Ministry of Labour and Employment at the Secretariat on Wednesday.
The meeting discussed the economic role of export processing zones (EPZs) and the implementation of laws and policies to preserve their distinct status while sustaining employment, Mahdi Amin said.
He said the government has been working to strengthen workers’ rights and would consider recommendations from international organisations such as the ITUC and IOE.
“Ensuring fair and safe workplaces, improving employer-worker relations and establishing effective social dialogue are among the government’s key priorities,” he said.
The government is also working to expand decent employment opportunities and develop the skills of the workforce, he added.
Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury was present at the meeting.
The visiting delegation included ITUC General Secretary Luc Triangle, IOE Vice-Chair Kaiser Moyane, ILO Governing Body member Jess Vogt and ILO Country Director Max Tunon, among others.
Welcoming the delegation, Mahdi Amin said the visit and tripartite discussions among the government, workers and employers would help assess progress and chart the way forward in implementing the ILO roadmap.
“Under the strong leadership of Tarique Rahman, the government is committed to workers’ welfare, decent work and productive employment,” he said.
Mahdi Amin said the newly elected government amended the Bangladesh Labour Act during the first session of parliament to bring it in line with current needs.
He said Bangladesh had recently ratified ILO Conventions 155, 187 and 189 to uphold international standards on workers’ rights and protection.
The government has also taken steps to strengthen labour administration, expedite dispute resolution and establish effective social dialogue among stakeholders, he added.
“Our main goal now is to quickly formulate the Bangladesh Labour Rules and ensure effective implementation of the amended Labour Act,” Mahdi Amin said.
He said the government was committed to turning its pledges into tangible improvements in the lives of workers.
The ITUC and IOE delegations praised recent labour-sector reforms, particularly amendments to the Labour Act, the streamlined trade union registration process, measures to improve occupational health and safety, and initiatives to ensure fair wages.

item.title: Benin full of pride at role in Messi's last dance
item.description:
Football fans in Benin declared that it was "an honour" that the west African nation provided the opposition for Lionel Messi's final international appearance -- and most only had eyes for the Argentinian superstar.
Benin lost 3-0 in Buenos Aires in front of more than 80,000 spectators on Tuesday -- but the result was almost meaningless on a night on which one of the world's greatest ever players made his international farewell.
From neighbourhood to neighbourhood, screens had sprung up in restaurants and bars in the Beninese capital Cotonou so as not to miss a moment of the historic occasion.
"We're looking for a screen, even if we have to stand," said one young worker, hurrying like many others to find a spot in time to watch the action from Argentina that kicked off at midnight local time in Benin.
Although a few "Go Benin" chants rang out during the national anthems, those watching in Benin really only had eyes for 39-year-old Messi, aware that they were witnessing a historic moment in world football.
"It's an honour that Benin is the last team Messi faces," said Sylvestre Dagbedji, 34, a security guard and self-declared Messi fan.
"We'll always remember that it was against Benin that he retired from international football," he added.
Sitting nearby, Armand Folly, 27, a motorcycle taxi driver, said: "It's going to be tough for us Beninese. Messi is a great player. I'm so proud of him for his career."
During the match, supporters cheered the Cheetahs' efforts to break through the Argentinian rearguard, but applauded the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner and former Barcelona forward every time he received the ball.
"I'm sad because Messi won't play anymore. He was excellent at Barca, I don't know who will be able to play like him again," said Toussain Kpadonou, a craftsman, who was gathered with around a hundred people in front of a giant screen.
The younger fans were also delighted to see the TV coverage of the final international appearance of a player who has lit up the football world for two decades.
"Messi is a god of football, the best player in the world. He performed so well throughout his entire career, from Barca to Inter Miami," said Destin Avere, 17.
In the 71st minute of the game, having already provided two assists, Messi stepped up to take the penalty to round out the score -- and the crowd in Benin erupted when the ball hit the back of the net.
Benin's defeat was already forgotten -- the crowd's only thought was for Messi. "We're going to miss him," said Armand Folly.

item.title: Deeds, not words
item.description:
Despite repeated warnings, condemnations, and assurances from political leaders and law enforcement agencies, the persistent links between political influence and crime continue to exist in Bangladesh.
Recent cases involving land grabbing, extortion, attacks, vandalism, and looting, with alleged links to activists from different political camps, are a deeply troubling reminder of this reality.
What is particularly concerning is how easily political identity can continue to overlap with criminal activity. Different parties may have vastly different ideologies and political agendas, but when political connections are used to provide protection, influence investigations, or enable criminal enterprises, the distinction becomes meaningless for ordinary citizens.
We agree with experts and civil society representatives that those directly involved as well as their patrons must be held accountable.
We have heard these demands before, however.
We have also heard repeated promises that criminals will not be protected because of their political affiliations.
Such statements are welcome, but statements alone cannot solve a problem that has persisted for years and appears capable of surviving changes in political power.
This is precisely why the current political leadership must demonstrate that this time will be different.
A change in government or political leadership should result in obvious, measurable changes in the nation's security and law-and-order situation. Citizens should not be expected to accept the same criminal networks, the same impunity, and the same abuses under a different political banner.
The government must therefore move beyond short-term arrests and disciplinary action. Investigations must identify masterminds and patrons, prosecutions must be impartial, and political parties must dismantle the structures that allow muscle power to flourish under their banners.
Bangladesh needs long-term institutional action, not another cycle of promises followed by familiar crimes. Political change must ultimately be felt in people's daily lives.
For citizens to believe that the country has truly entered a new chapter, the rule of law must become stronger, more consistent, and unmistakably independent of political influence.

item.title: Subsidies must reach the poor
item.description:
The World Bank’s latest findings expose a serious weakness in how subsidies and social safety-net programs are designed and delivered, with large amounts of public money failing to reach the poorest households.
This is not simply a question of inefficiency; it is a question of fairness. A system that allows wealthier households to capture a substantial share of electricity, fuel, and other subsidies while vulnerable families remain excluded is fundamentally failing in its purpose.
With poverty rising and household purchasing power under pressure, we can no longer afford to spend scarce public resources without ensuring that they produce the greatest possible benefit for those who need them.
The government must therefore undertake a serious overhaul of the system. Fragmented programs, overlapping beneficiary lists, and weak targeting must be replaced with a unified, transparent mechanism for identifying vulnerable households.
Subsidies must also become more targeted: Instead of providing broad benefits that disproportionately favour those who consume more, public funds should be directed towards households that genuinely require assistance. Cash transfers and food support should be expanded where evidence shows they can deliver greater impact, while leakages and politically influenced beneficiary selection must be eliminated.
Most importantly, reform must be measurable. The government should publish clear targets for coverage, exclusion, and leakage, and regularly report whether the poorest households are actually receiving support.
Economic hardship should not become a permanent disadvantage for the most vulnerable. Bangladesh's social protection system must stop rewarding those who are already better off and start delivering meaningful protection to those at greatest risk of being left behind.
Bangladesh cannot claim to have an effective social protection system when those who need support the most are routinely being left out.

item.title: What each investor in New York could build in Bangladesh
item.description:
Most investor meetings produce a photograph. The breakfast JP Morgan hosted in New York in the last week of September produced something rarer: A guest list that doubles as a plan. BlackRock, PIMCO, TPG, Macquarie, I Squared, Farallon, Jane Street, GoldenTree, and MetLife sat across from Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, with six other institutions alongside them.
Those names are not a random sample of Wall Street. Together they cover the sovereign bond Bangladesh wants to launch, the infrastructure it needs to build, and the credit its industries need to grow. Someone drew up that list knowing exactly what Bangladesh has to finance over the next decade.
The rest of the week filled in the picture. At a VEON and Banglalink symposium, the finance minister announced approval of a digital bank licence backed by VEON, Banglalink, and Square Group. In California, State Minister Shama Obaed Islam and ICT Adviser Rehan Asif Asad met chip engineers and the founders of Zscaler and Replit, and opened talks with Arizona State University on chip-design education. In four days, Bangladesh spoke to the bond market, the builders of hard assets, and the technology frontier.
Begin with the bond, because everything else borrows against it. The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has approved in principle JP Morgan as lead manager for Bangladesh's first international issue, with $500m to $1bn under discussion.
Look at who was in the room. PIMCO is one of the largest fixed-income managers in the world. GoldenTree lives on credit. MetLife carries liabilities that stretch decades ahead and needs assets that stretch just as far. Jane Street makes markets in emerging-market bonds and the funds that hold them, the plumbing that keeps a new issue trading after launch day. BlackRock runs some of the largest emerging-market debt portfolios anywhere.
That is an anchor order book and a secondary market in a single sitting. A debut that prices tightly does more than raise a billion dollars. It hands every Bangladeshi bank, utility, and exporter a benchmark to borrow against for a generation.
Then come the builders, and here the match is almost uncanny. Macquarie manages more infrastructure assets than any firm on earth, from ports to renewable power. I Squared has assembled power and utility assets across Asia. TPG runs a climate fund built for energy transition in emerging markets. BlackRock bought Global Infrastructure Partners in 2024 and now competes in the same arena.
Bangladesh has a shovel-ready need for each. Chittagong and Matarbari need port capacity. The grid needs transmission and storage to carry the renewable power already on the drawing board. Data centres need electricity and fibre. Farallon, with its depth in private credit, could finance the mid-sized industrial and logistics firms that Bangladeshi banks struggle to serve at scale. Little of this shows up in headline foreign investment figures. All of it shows up in the skyline.
The California track supplies the ingredient that grows faster than money: People. Ulkasemi, a TSMC Design Centre Alliance partner, employs more than 600 engineers across four countries. sBIT designs chips for clients including Broadcom and AMD. Arizona State University hosts one of the largest engineering schools in the United States.
Bangladesh does not need a wafer fab to matter in semiconductors. It needs to multiply the design and verification work it already does well, and it has just met the partners who could help.
The numbers behind the pitch have not looked this good in years. Remittances reached a record $35.56bn in the fiscal year to June, up 17.3%. Usable reserves exceed $31bn, close to five months of imports.
Moody's lifted its outlook to stable in September, citing reduced political and external pressure after the February election. UNCTAD recorded the fastest growth in foreign direct investment in South Asia in 2025, at 45%.
To a bond buyer, remittances anchor the external account. To a builder, a market of more than 180 million people whose appetite for power, logistics and housing runs far ahead of supply is the entire thesis.
History is blunt about what happens next. Costa Rica's investment agency CINDE held about 19 meetings with Intel before the company committed $115m in 1997. Within 15 years that became roughly $900m and Intel was the country's largest exporter. Samsung has invested $23.2bn in Vietnam since 1995. In both cases the first meeting changed nothing. The nineteenth changed everything.
So the follow-through could be written investor by investor. For the bond buyers, a quarterly letter from the finance minister on reform milestones, published before the roadshow, would let the debut arrive with a track record attached.
For the builders, Invest Bangladesh could assemble a dozen investment-ready projects in energy, logistics and digital infrastructure, each with a data room, a named owner and a clear risk-sharing structure. Macquarie cannot underwrite a slide. It can underwrite a project. For the credit houses, a guarantee facility for mid-sized exporters could unlock lending at a scale the banking system alone cannot reach.
For the technology track, a memorandum with Arizona State University, a fast-track window for chip and AI firms, and a diaspora fellowship that brings senior engineers home for six-month stints would turn a visit into a channel.
Above all, each of the 15 institutions could be given one named senior counterpart in Dhaka and a promise of answers within a fortnight. Serious investors read response time as a proxy for everything else.
The prime minister has set his sights on a $1 trillion economy by 2034. From about $500bn today, that requires roughly 6% real growth sustained for eight years. A steady course of 4.5% lands near $830bn. An investment breakout at 7.5% reaches about $1.17tn.
The gap between those paths is some $340bn of annual output, more than half the size of today's economy. Geography will not close it. Demography will not close it. The capital that sat at that table could.
The guest list in New York already reads like a blueprint. The job now is to show each name, firm by firm, exactly where it fits.
Ashfaq Zaman is Chief Strategist of the Dhaka Forum Initiative, a Dhaka-based policy think tank. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Who invests in the people we ask to lead?
item.description:
In conversations about public services and local governance in Bangladesh, I often hear a familiar request: “Can you speak to the MP, the mayor, or someone in the party?”
The issue may be a road, a hospital service or an office that has not responded. People turn to political figures because they hope someone with influence can make the system work.
That expectation reveals something about our institutions. Citizens should not need personal access to a politician to receive a public service.
Yet, politicians are often expected to take calls, attend events, resolve individual problems, and remain visible every day.
We also expect them to understand budgets, oversee institutions, and make decisions that improve lives.
When do we give them the time and support to learn how to do all of that well?
We have become comfortable praising political sacrifice. Some leaders give up considerable time with family and little of their day belongs entirely to them. But exhaustion is a poor measure of public service.
A politician who is available to everyone at every hour may still have too little time to study a proposal, consult those affected by it, or plan beyond the next urgent request.
None of this reduces the need for scrutiny. Politicians hold power and must answer for their decisions, conduct, and use of public resources.
There is, however, a difference between questioning a decision and targeting someone’s family or private life.
Intimidation can make participation in politics unsafe. In a 2026 Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) survey, 71% of responding MPs reported experiencing violence from the public -- online, offline, or both.
The report also describes effects on family members and on some MPs’ willingness to appear publicly or seek another term. These are international findings, not a Bangladesh estimate.
The risks are not shared equally. Another 2025 IPU study on Asia-Pacific found that 60% of the women parliamentarians interviewed had experienced online gender-based violence. A 2026 UN brief documents violence against women politicians, candidates and party members in Bangladesh across electoral, party, institutional, and digital spaces.
Any serious discussion of political leadership must consider who can afford to remain visible, and at what personal cost.
Yet, concern for politicians’ safety must be matched by concern for the safety of people who encounter them.
Recent allegations of sexual abuse involving political actors are a reminder that public influence can be misused.
An allegation requires a fair process; it should neither be dismissed because of someone’s position nor treated as a finding of guilt.
People reporting harm need safe ways to come forward, protection from retaliation and access to appropriate support.
Political parties and public institutions need procedures that can examine complaints independently and act on substantiated misconduct.
International parliamentary guidance recommends confidential, fair complaints mechanisms and sanctions following thorough investigation.
This is why safeguarding and integrity belong within political capacity building.
Leaders need to understand professional boundaries, conflicts of interest, consent, the risks created by unequal power and their duty to prevent harassment and exploitation.
But training alone cannot keep integrity intact. Clear standards, independent reporting routes and consequences for violations are essential.
We cannot ask the public to trust politicians’ judgment while leaving people vulnerable to their misuse of power.
Political capacity also means learning how to serve effectively. I do not mean foreign travel, conference photographs, or training events made impressive by protocol.
Learning should be judged by whether it helps a leader engage more honestly, exercise power responsibly, and deliver better results.
A newly elected representative should be able to develop a workplan for the term ahead. What do residents identify as priorities? Which matters fall within the representative’s authority? Which requires cooperation with other institutions? What can reasonably change in one year, and what will take longer? How will people know whether progress has been made?
Those questions are particularly useful in Bangladesh, where a politician may receive requests ranging from an individual hospital referral to a recurring failure in local public services.
Responding to one person may be necessary. Recognizing the pattern, bringing the responsible agencies together, and pressing for a durable solution requires different skills. It also requires a way to record requests, follow them up, and report back to constituents.
Managing expectations matters just as much. Citizens deserve to know what their representative can do, what another institution must do, and why a promise may take time to fulfil.
That calls for listening, honesty, and the confidence to explain a limit without dismissing the person who needs help.
Leaders must also keep learning about the world in which decisions are made. Economic pressures, climate risks, public health needs, digital misinformation, and technological change do not wait for the next election. Political experience is valuable, but it cannot keep anyone current on every issue.
A Monash University research on parliamentary induction has found that many programs relied on information and handbooks rather than active skill development. Although that study is older and does not assess Bangladesh’s present institutions, it raises the right question: Are leaders given opportunities to practise the work we ask them to perform?
Responsibility begins with political parties. They recruit and nominate candidates and shape how members understand leadership. They should invest their own resources in policy knowledge, ethics, safeguarding, communication, and constituency engagement.
They must also establish credible ways to respond when members are accused of abusing their position. These responsibilities begin well before an election and continue afterward.
Public institutions have a different responsibility. The Bangladesh Parliament Secretariat should support MPs from every party with research, induction, and continuing learning for legislation, oversight and representation, alongside clear standards of conduct.
There is a foundation to build on: The Secretariat and UNDP held an orientation for more than 300 newly elected MPs in June 2026. Local representatives need support suited to their responsibilities. The National Institute of Local Government already provides training for local government actors and resources on planning.
Universities, researchers, and civil society can bring evidence and community perspectives into these efforts. The Election Commission’s role should remain narrower: Helping candidates and parties understand electoral rules while preserving its neutrality.
The measure of success should be visible to citizens. Did a representative publish a credible workplan? Are requests followed up? Can people understand why a decision was made? Can someone report misconduct without fearing the political influence of the person involved?
A certificate or a study tour answers none of these questions. Investing in politicians’ capacity is not an appeal to be less demanding of them. It is a way to make our demands more meaningful.
Parties should prepare people to lead and answer for their conduct; public institutions should equip those who take office and uphold fair standards; and citizens should be able to judge what they deliver.
We ask politicians to solve institutional problems through personal availability. Bangladesh would gain more from leaders who have the time, skills, and integrity to strengthen those institutions -- and from safeguards that protect people when leaders fail to meet those standards.
SM Shaikat is Executive Director of SERAC-Bangladesh and an international policy analyst.

item.title: The AI story is really a human story
item.description:
At the Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026, I found myself listening for one word.
The opening discussion was about power, technology and trust in an age of uncertainty. As expected, there was plenty about technology -- especially artificial intelligence -- and about how governments and world leaders are struggling to respond to a technology that is moving faster than the rules around it.
But I kept waiting for the third word: Trust . How is trust built? How does it disappear? And perhaps most importantly, who gets to shape either process?
Walking out of that session, I felt that these questions were more important than the technology itself. AI does not build trust or destroy it by itself. People build it. People destroy it. People decide how technology is designed, who controls it, and what purposes it serves.
The historian of technology Melvin Kranzberg made this point decades ago. His first law famously said: “Technology is neither good nor bad; nor is it neutral.” His sixth was even more direct: “Technology is a very human activity.”
That observation feels remarkably current in the age of AI.
We have seen this before, close to home. As I thought about it, my mind went to Ramu. In late September 2012, a photograph depicting the desecration of the Quran appeared on Facebook and was linked to a young Buddhist man in Ramu, Cox's Bazar. He denied posting it.
The story spread rapidly, and on September 29-30 mobs attacked the Buddhist community. In Ramu alone, at least 12 Buddhist temples and monasteries and more than 50 houses were destroyed. A later judicial inquiry exonerated the young man, concluding that he had been a victim of the misuse of social media. The violence also spread beyond Ramu.
Six years later, the pattern appeared on a much larger scale, just across the border. In its 2018 report on Myanmar, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission described the role of social media as “significant” and said Facebook had become a useful instrument for those seeking to spread hate, in a country where, for many users, Facebook was effectively the internet. The mission also noted that the real-world effects of Facebook posts and messages needed independent examination.
Neither of these was an AI story. Both were human stories in which a powerful communication technology met fear, grievance and people willing to exploit them.
Generative AI changes the equation because it can make deception cheaper, faster and more convincing. A fabricated voice, image or video can now be produced and distributed at enormous scale.
But the appetite for deception is not new. Research tells us something unsettling about why such material travels. In a 2018 study published in Science , Soroush Vosoughi, Deb Roy and Sinan Aral analyzed roughly 126,000 verified true and false news stories shared on Twitter between 2006 and 2017.
False stories were 70% more likely to be retweeted than true ones. And when the researchers accounted for bots, the difference remained: Human behaviour, not automated accounts, explained the greater spread of falsehood. False stories also generated more reactions associated with surprise, fear and disgust.
That should make us pause. The problem may not always be convincing people of one particular lie. Sometimes it may simply be keeping people sufficiently angry, surprised or afraid that they stop trusting what is in front of them.
Trust is a social product
This is where I think the AI debate often becomes too technical. Robert Putnam, in Bowling Alone , explained that people are more likely to trust when they actually know one another, interact regularly and belong to communities where behaviour has consequences.
Francis Fukuyama made a related argument in Trust, defining trust as an expectation of regular, honest and cooperative behaviour based on shared norms, and linking it to the ability of societies to work together and prosper.
That makes me wonder what happens when our social lives become increasingly mediated by screens. A phone can give us an extraordinary amount of information without giving us the relationships needed to test that information. A feed can tell us what millions of strangers are saying while removing us from the neighbour sitting across the street.
The 2026 Edelman Trust Barometer offers a striking picture of this problem. Based on a survey of 33,938 people across 28 countries, it found that 70% of respondents were unwilling or hesitant to trust someone whose values, information sources, approaches to social issues or cultural background differed from their own.
Edelman describes this condition as “insularity.” It also reports that the gap in its trust index between high- and low-income respondents has widened from six points in 2012 to 15 points in 2026.
These are not measurements of AI. They are measurements of us. And they suggest something important: A society already divided by identity, insecurity and distrust is easier to manipulate with any powerful communication technology, whether it is Facebook in 2012 or generative AI today.
Who controls the tool?
This brings me to the question underneath the AI regulation debate: Who controls the technology? In Power and Progress , economists Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson argue that technological progress does not automatically distribute its benefits widely.
The direction of technological change depends on choices, institutions and who has the power to make those choices. Technology can serve broad prosperity, but it can also serve narrow interests.
Their wider work with James Robinson on institutions made a similar point. In awarding the three economists the 2024 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, the Nobel committee cited their research on how institutions are formed and affect prosperity.
It distinguishes inclusive institutions, in which people have a meaningful stake in governance, from extractive institutions in which political and economic power is concentrated in a narrow elite.
That distinction matters enormously for AI. Frontier AI is not being developed in a world where everyone has equal access to computing power, data, specialized talent and capital.
Stanford's 2026 AI Index reports that industry produced more than 90% of notable frontier models in 2025. A UK government assessment similarly notes that frontier development requires such substantial funding, skills, data and computation that it is likely to remain concentrated among a small group of companies.
The concentration of wealth is part of this story too. Oxfam's January 2026 report says billionaire wealth rose by more than 16% in 2025, reaching $18.3 trillion. It estimates that billionaires are more than 4,000 times more likely than ordinary citizens to hold political office, and says the wealth of the poorest half of humanity is smaller than that of the world's 12 richest billionaires.
These are Oxfam's estimates, based on its own methodology, so they should be read in that context. But they illustrate the scale of the concentration of resources and political access that now surrounds some of the world's most powerful technologies.
The difficult question, then, is not simply whether AI is powerful. It is whether institutions are strong enough to make sure that extraordinary power remains accountable.
Regulation cannot do everything
None of this means that we should stop regulating AI. We need rules around transparency, accountability, data protection and synthetic media. Governments will have to decide how to deal with deepfakes, automated decision-making and the growing power of the companies building these systems. But regulation operates inside society. It does not float above it.
If institutions are trusted, rules have a better chance of working. If institutions are weak, divided or captured by powerful interests, even well-designed rules can become instruments of selective enforcement. That is why I keep coming back to something much older than AI: The strength of the social fabric around us.
People need real communities to belong to -- public spaces, libraries, playgrounds, clubs, neighbourhood organizations, and campuses where people encounter others who do not necessarily think like them.
People also need things that make life worth looking up from the screen for: Affordable culture, sport, music and recreation. Otherwise, the endless feed becomes the easiest form of escape.
We need institutions that reward merit rather than loyalty, whether in public service, business or politics. And we need something even more basic for young people: A believable path into the future.
Hope works better when there is a pathway behind it. None of these things sounds particularly high-tech. Perhaps that is precisely the point.
The question I left with
The AI debate will continue. Models will become more capable. Regulation will evolve. Companies and governments will keep competing over technology, data, infrastructure and influence. But however powerful AI becomes, the consequences will still depend on human choices.
That is why, after listening to a panel about power, technology and trust, I found myself thinking less about whether we can trust AI. The more difficult question is whether we still trust one another -- and whether our institutions have given us enough reason to do so. The AI story is a human story. And, in the end, so is its ending.
Aminul Ehsan is a democracy, governance and political parties expert.

item.title: Building a better Bangladesh: Protecting women’s health in a changing climate
item.description:
Bangladesh has become a remarkable example of development resilience, with consistent, significant improvements in economic and other human development indicators. Climate change is increasingly threatening many of these hard-earned gains, particularly in the country’s coastal regions. Rising sea levels, salinity intrusion, cyclones, flooding, prolonged heat, and erratic rainfall are no longer distant environmental concerns—they have become everyday realities for millions of people. While climate change affects entire communities, women and girls often bear a disproportionate share of the burden because of existing social, economic, and cultural inequalities. Gender disparities in climate impacts, particularly on women’s health, are rarely discussed in national and global policy forums.
Climate change is also a public health challenge
Bangladesh is among the countries most exposed to climate-related hazards. Nearly 40 million people live in Bangladesh’s coastal zone, where climate change is already affecting agriculture, freshwater availability, livelihoods, and public health (Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100; World Bank, 2022). Climate discussions frequently focus on damaged embankments, agricultural losses, disappearing livelihoods, or infrastructure resilience. These are undoubtedly important. However, an equally urgent crisis often remains invisible -- the impact of climate change on women’s health.
Across coastal Bangladesh, environmental changes influence nearly every aspect of women's daily lives. Women travel longer distances to collect drinking water when water near their homes becomes saline, care for sick family members during climate-related illnesses, manage households under increasingly difficult conditions, and often sacrifice their own health needs to ensure that other family members are cared for first. Floods and cyclones restrict their mobility, often forcing them to forgo healthcare.
Their unpaid care work is rarely counted in economic statistics, yet it quietly supports community resilience during every climate shock. Studies have consistently shown that women spend significantly more time than men on unpaid care and domestic work, particularly during and after climate-related disasters, limiting their opportunities for education, paid employment, and healthcare (UN Women, 2023; ILO, 2022).
When pregnancy becomes more dangerous
One of the clearest examples of climate-related health vulnerability can be seen during pregnancy. During the monsoon season or after cyclones, roads may become impassable, boats may stop operating, and health facilities may be several hours away. Even when services remain available, transportation costs often increase beyond what poorer households can afford. So, these women are frequently deprived of essential maternal healthcare, including antenatal care, delivery with skilled attendants, and emergency obstetric services, risking their lives.
Additionally, research conducted in coastal Bangladesh has linked increasing salinity in drinking water with elevated sodium intake among pregnant women, contributing to higher risks of gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia (Khan et al., 2011; WHO, 2024).
In Bangladesh, the maternal mortality ratio declined from approximately 434 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2000 to around 123 in recent estimates—one of South Asia’s major public health success stories (WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank, & UNDESA, 2023). Protecting these achievements now requires recognizing climate resilience as an integral component of maternal healthcare. Health systems must be prepared not only to respond after disasters but also to ensure continuity of essential reproductive and maternal health services before, during, and after climate events.
The silent burden of menstrual health
In many climate-vulnerable communities, access to safe water, sanitation facilities, and privacy becomes increasingly difficult during floods, cyclones, or periods of prolonged water scarcity. Girls and women often struggle to maintain menstrual hygiene when toilets are damaged, freshwater is unavailable, or sanitary products become unaffordable.
For adolescent girls, these challenges extend beyond physical discomfort. Feelings of embarrassment, anxiety, and fear frequently accompany menstruation, particularly when schools lack adequate sanitation facilities or when displacement forces families into crowded shelters with limited privacy.
Some girls choose to miss school during menstruation. Others reduce food or water intake to avoid using inadequate toilets, negatively affecting their educational participation, confidence, and overall well-being.
These experiences remind us that climate adaptation is not only about strengthening embankments or improving disaster forecasting. It is also about ensuring dignity, privacy, and basic health needs for women and girls.
Mental health deserves equal attention
The psychological consequences of climate change receive far less attention than physical health impacts. Again, women are disproportionately affected by the care burden, limited access to maternal and menstrual health, on top of the financial worries created by climate change. Mothers often carry the emotional burden of ensuring food security, caring for children and older family members, and managing household responsibilities under increasingly uncertain conditions. Repeated or prolonged climate change often forces young family members to migrate, leaving women with greater caregiving responsibilities.
This constant uncertainty can contribute to anxiety, emotional exhaustion, and depression. Yet mental health services remain limited, particularly in rural coastal areas where specialized support is often unavailable.
Climate adaptation must become gender-responsive
Bangladesh has earned international recognition for reducing disaster-related mortality through investments in early warning systems, cyclone shelters, and community preparedness. However, the next generation of climate adaptation requires a broader understanding of resilience.
Resilience is not measured only by the number of embankments constructed or cyclone shelters built. It is equally reflected in whether pregnant women can safely reach healthcare during emergencies, whether adolescent girls can continue attending school with dignity, whether families have reliable access to clean drinking water, and whether women can recover physically and emotionally after disasters. In other words, climate resilience must be people-centered, gender-responsive, and health-focused.
Women as leaders of climate resilience
Conversations about climate vulnerability often portray women primarily as victims. But, across Bangladesh, women are also among the country’s most important agents of resilience.
In coastal villages, women have developed countless ways of adapting to changing environmental conditions. They carefully manage scarce freshwater, diversify household income through home-based enterprises, preserve food during periods of uncertainty, support neighbors during disasters, and ensure children continue their education despite repeated disruptions. Women’s participation as community health volunteers, teachers, and local government representatives is critical in disaster preparedness and recovery.
Yet these contributions often remain invisible in planning and decision-making. Women remain underrepresented in many local adaptation and mitigation committees. Policies designed without women’s perspectives risk overlooking the realities of everyday life in climate-vulnerable communities.
Investing in health is investing in resilience
Mass immunization, community-based healthcare, maternal health programs, and improvements in primary healthcare have contributed significantly to the country’s development progress. Climate change now demands that these investments evolve.
Healthcare systems must become climate resilient by ensuring uninterrupted essential services during environmental emergencies. This includes maintaining maternal healthcare, reproductive health services, vaccination programs, nutrition support, mental health care, and access to safe water and sanitation even during floods, cyclones, and prolonged heatwaves.
Digital health technologies, mobile outreach services, community clinics, and trained frontline health workers can all play an important role in reaching vulnerable populations when conventional services are disrupted. Equally important is ensuring that climate adaptation funding explicitly includes health system strengthening rather than treating health as a secondary concern.
Protecting women’s health should not be viewed as a sectoral issue confined to the Ministry of Health. It is closely connected to agriculture, education, water management, social protection, local governance, disaster risk reduction, and economic development. A healthier population is better equipped to withstand climate shocks, recover from disasters, and contribute productively to society.
Five priorities for building Bangladesh better
As Bangladesh prepares for an increasingly uncertain climate future, five priorities deserve particular attention.
First, integrate women’s health into climate adaptation planning. National and local climate strategies should explicitly address maternal health, reproductive healthcare, menstrual health, nutrition, mental wellbeing, and gender-based violence as core components of resilience. Health indicators should be included alongside infrastructure and environmental targets.
Second, strengthen climate-resilient primary healthcare. Community clinics and primary health centers should be equipped to continue delivering essential services during disasters. This includes emergency transportation, reliable electricity, safe water, adequate medical supplies, and trained personnel capable of responding to climate-related health challenges.
Third, improve water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure. Access to clean water and safe sanitation remains fundamental for women’s health. Investments in climate-resilient WASH infrastructure should prioritize schools, healthcare facilities, cyclone shelters, and remote communities where women and girls face the greatest barriers.
Fourth, expand women’s participation in climate governance. Women should have meaningful representation on disaster management committees, in local government planning, in water resource management, and in climate adaptation initiatives. Their lived experiences provide valuable knowledge that can improve policy effectiveness.
Finally, strengthen social protection for climate-vulnerable households. Climate shocks often deepen poverty and force families into difficult coping strategies. Responsive and inclusive social protection programs can reduce financial insecurity while helping women maintain access to healthcare, nutritious food, education, and essential services during times of crisis.
A whole-of-society approach
No single institution can address the complex relationship between climate change and women’s health. Government agencies, development partners, research institutions, civil society organizations, local governments, and communities all have important roles to play.
Researchers can generate evidence that informs better policy. Universities can train the next generation of public health and climate professionals. Civil society organizations can amplify community voices and strengthen accountability. The private sector can contribute through innovation in health technologies, clean water solutions, and sustainable infrastructure. Development partners can support long-term investments that prioritize locally led adaptation.
Most importantly, communities themselves must remain at the center of decision-making. Policies are strongest when they reflect the realities, priorities, and aspirations of the people they are intended to serve.
Building Bangladesh better means leaving no woman behind
Bangladesh’s future will not be determined solely by economic growth, modern infrastructure, or technological advancement. It will also depend on whether development remains inclusive, equitable, and resilient in the face of growing climate uncertainty.
Women living in climate-vulnerable regions are not asking for extraordinary privileges. They seek reliable healthcare, clean drinking water, safe sanitation, secure livelihoods, accessible transportation during emergencies, and opportunities to participate in decisions that affect their lives. These are not only fundamental rights but also essential foundations of sustainable development.
Protecting women's health is therefore not an additional item on the development agenda. It is central to achieving many of Bangladesh’s national aspirations, including improved public health, greater gender equality, stronger local governance, enhanced climate resilience, and sustained economic progress.
The theme of Building Bangladesh Better invites us to imagine the kind of nation we want to create over the coming decades. It is an opportunity to move beyond rebuilding after disasters and instead invest in systems that protect people before crises occur. It challenges us to recognize that resilience is not measured only by stronger roads, embankments, or buildings, but also by healthier mothers, confident adolescent girls, accessible healthcare, and communities where every individual can thrive despite environmental change.
By placing women’s health at the heart of climate adaptation, Bangladesh can safeguard decades of development progress while building a future that is not only stronger and more resilient, but also more just, inclusive, and compassionate.
Md Al-Mamun is a Research Associate at the BRAC Institute of Governance and Development (BIGD), BRAC University. He can be reached at md.mamun@bracu.ac.bd
Marufa Alam is a Lecturer in the Department of Public and Community Health at Frontier University Garowe, Somalia. She can be reached at marufa@frontier.edu.so

item.title: France suspends use of stun grenades against protesters
item.description:
France is suspending the use of stun grenades at student-led protests as people report allegations of police brutality at demonstrations that have widened over the weeks.
“I am suspending their use in the high school student protests until the facts of the incident have been clarified,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told RTL radio broadcaster on Wednesday.
He emphasized that the suspension was “only for the high school student protests” and for “just long enough to understand what happened.”
Nunez announced the measure to curb growing anger after reports of serious injuries to teenage protesters drew public anger.
French regional newspaper La Voix du Nord reported this Monday that a 15-year-old had his hand and a part of his lower arm blown off after picking up a police stun grenade that then detonated during protests.
Last week, a 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the jaw as a tear gas canister was fired during protests, with the officer having been charged on Tuesday.
Wednesday’s order comes before an address by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to protesters later Wednesday evening.
The demonstrations are also taking place at a difficult time for the French government as it tries to rein in its debts while facing demands to spend more on public services.
Protests first began mid-September in the Paris region after students began mobilizing against perceived inequalities in the education system.
From the outset, pupils said teaching, facilities and opportunities for advancement weren’t as good for students in disadvantaged neighborhoods — despite the promise of France’s national motto of “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”
Demonstrations then spread to all parts of the country, including smaller towns with high schools.
On Tuesday, trade unions joined student protests. The Interior Ministry said nearly 256,000 people took part in protests nationwide on Tuesday.
Protests turned violent in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square toward the end.
More than 6,500 people have been arrested over the course of the last two weeks, most of them minors.

item.title: IUBAT hosts two-day International Conference 'BECITHCON 2026'
item.description:
The 2026 IEEE International Conference on Biomedical Engineering, Computer and Information Technology for Health (BECITHCON 2026) concluded on Wednesday at the International University of Business Agriculture and Technology (IUBAT).
The IEEE Bangladesh Section and the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBS) Bangladesh Chapter jointly organized the conference, with IUBAT as the host institution. It brought together researchers, academics, physicians, engineers, industry professionals and students from Bangladesh and abroad.
Professor Dr Abdur Rab, vice chancellor of IUBAT, served as chief adviser. Professor Dr Shaikh Anowarul Fattah, professor of EEE at BUET and chair of the IEEE EMBS Bangladesh Chapter, served as TPC chair, while Dr Celia Shahnaz, professor of EEE at BUET and vice chair of the IEEE EMBS Bangladesh Chapter, served as general chair.
Professor Dr Mohammed Imamul Hassan Bhuiyan, professor of EEE at BUET and chair of the IEEE Bangladesh Section, and Professor Dr Md Monirul Islam, professor and head of the Department of Civil Engineering at IUBAT, served as organizing chairs.
Dr Khadiza Akter, associate professor and coordinator of the Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering (EEE) at IUBAT and TPC secretary of BECITHCON 2026, delivered the welcome address.
The conference featured international researchers and speakers, including several IEEE Fellows. The program included 8 invited lectures, 31 technical sessions and a Technical Expert Forum covering developments in biomedical engineering, artificial intelligence, healthcare technology, medical imaging, biomedical devices and health informatics.
An IEEE Humanitarian Technology Program was also held as part of the conference, highlighting technology-based solutions for community development and improved quality of life.
The closing session was chaired by Professor Selina Nargis, chief patron, treasurer and director of Administration of IUBAT, who delivered the vote of thanks to the organizers, authors, session chairs, participants and contributors.
The organizers presented Best Paper Awards for outstanding research contributions during the closing ceremony.
The organizers expressed hope that BECITHCON 2026 will foster international research collaboration and inspire young researchers to contribute to technology-driven healthcare innovation in Bangladesh and beyond.

item.title: BUFT National Entrepreneurship Expo 2026 opens
item.description:

Organized by the BUFT Business Club in association with the Faculty of Business Studies (FBS), the 2-day expo is being held on October 7-8 under the theme “Empowering the Next Generation with AI: Entrepreneurship, Innovation, and Sustainable Digital Transformation.”
The expo aims to equip students with entrepreneurial skills and encourage them to harness AI and emerging technologies for innovative and sustainable ventures.
Among the distinguished guests were BUFT Chairman of the Board of Trustees Md Mesbha Uddin Ali, Vice Chancellor Prof Dr Engr Ayub Nabi Khan, Member of the Board of Governors of Spectrum International University College, Malaysia and PRAN-RFL Group Director Prof Dr Mohamed Kaisarul Haq, and Acting Pro-Vice Chancellor and Treasurer Prof Dr Md Alamgir Hossain.
Dean of the Faculty of Business Studies Prof Dr Sheikh Abdur Rahim and other BUFT deans and heads also attended the opening and various sessions.
The expo offers students opportunities to connect with industry professionals, explore business ideas and gain practical insights into entrepreneurship, innovation and the growing role of AI in the future of work and enterprise.
The expo will continue on October 8 with further activities focused on developing students’ creativity, entrepreneurial capabilities and digital readiness.

item.title: realme C100 launched with 8,000mAh battery
item.description:
realme has officially launched its much-anticipated C-series smartphone, the ‘all-round durable champion’ realme C100, in Bangladesh.
The device revolutionizes battery backup and performance in its segment, combining long-lasting power, enhanced durability, water resistance, and smooth performance to keep up with users’ all-round needs.

item.title: Fire breaks out at Mumbai film city
item.description:
A fire broke out at a temporary shooting setup at Mumbai’s Film City in Goregaon East on Monday, October 5, damaging electrical equipment and other production materials. No injuries were reported.
According to the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) and Mumbai Fire Brigade, the fire was reported at 4:02pm near Reliance MediaWorks and behind Prime Focus Studio in Film City. The incident was classified as a Level I fire.
The fire was contained to part of a temporary structure housing a production control unit, according to the fire brigade’s preliminary report. Electrical wiring, cables, doors, wooden boards, air-conditioning equipment, bamboo and plastic materials, sound equipment and other production items were damaged.
Firefighters, police, BMC ward control officials and personnel from the 108 ambulance service responded to the incident. The fire was brought under control by 4:55pm.
Ashok Dubey, president of the All India Film Employees Confederation (AIFEC) and general secretary of the Federation of Western India Cine Employees (FWICE), said the fire started on the outer shade of a temporary setup used for Pati Patni Aur Panga 2 . Smoke also spread toward nearby sets, including Hustle 5 and Kaun Banega Crorepati .
The incident initially led to reports that the set of Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana had caught fire. However, subsequent reports said the fire did not occur on the Ramayana set.
The fire disrupted production at nearby television sets. Reports said the Hustle 5 finale and Kaun Banega Crorepati shoots were halted temporarily as smoke reached the locations.
The cause of the fire has not been confirmed.
Ramayana , directed by Nitesh Tiwari, stars Ranbir Kapoor as Ram, Sai Pallavi as Sita, Yash as Ravana and Sunny Deol as Hanuman. The cast also includes Ravie Dubey, Arun Govil and others. The Daily Star has previously used these spellings for the principal cast, while Filmfare lists Ravie Dubey as Lakshman.
The film’s first installment is scheduled for a Diwali 2026 release.

item.title: Rowan Atkinson to revive ‘Mr Bean,’ ‘Blackadder’ on West End Stage
item.description:
Rowan Atkinson will return to London’s West End next year with Rowan Live , a new stage show featuring sketches and characters from his best-known comedy works.
The limited season will run at the Gillian Lynne Theatre from February 8 to March 13. The show will feature material from Mr Bean , Blackadder and Not the Nine O’Clock News , alongside new sketches.
Atkinson will reunite with longtime collaborators, including writer Richard Curtis, Blackadder co-creator Ben Elton, and composer Howard Goodall.
The show marks Atkinson’s return to the West End comedy sketch format after four decades.
“It is forty years since I last did a comedy sketch show in the West End,” Atkinson said, adding that he wanted to revisit the sketches that began his collaboration with Curtis and introduced some of his best-known characters.
Atkinson first performed with Curtis on stage in the 1970s. Their work later contributed to some of British television’s most popular comedies, including Not the Nine O’Clock News .
He went on to star as Edmund Blackadder in Blackadder and as the largely silent Mr Bean, two characters that became defining roles in his career.
Curtis, who first saw Atkinson perform in 1976, described him as a “unique, once-in-a-lifetime talent” and said his comic ability remained unchanged decades later.
The production will be directed by Raz Shaw, with music by Goodall.
Rowan Live will combine Atkinson’s established characters with new material written specifically for the production.

item.title: UNESCO, Windmill partner to take Bangladesh’s rickshaw painting global
item.description:
Bangladesh’s traditional rickshaw painting is set to gain greater international exposure through a new partnership aimed at promoting the folk art globally and creating new opportunities for its artists.
UNESCO and Windmill Advertising Limited signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on Wednesday at the UNESCO Dhaka Office to advance the initiative. Dr Susan Vize, Head of Office and UNESCO Representative to Bangladesh, signed the agreement on behalf of UNESCO, while Schumonn Patwary, Chief Strategic Planner of Windmill Advertising Limited, signed for the company.
Representatives of UNESCO and Windmill Advertising Limited hold the memorandum of understanding (MoU) after signing the agreement to promote Bangladesh’s Rickshaw Art. Photo: Courtesy
“Rickshaw Painting is a living tradition sustained by the knowledge, skills and creativity of artists. The artists themselves are the driving force behind keeping this art form alive. Through this partnership between UNESCO and Windmill, we will support artists’ livelihoods and help them pass their skills on to younger generations so that the tradition continues to thrive,” said Vize.
Patwary said: “Through this partnership, we aim to preserve the rich heritage of Bangladesh’s Rickshaw Art while creating new opportunities and possibilities for the artists associated with it. Our goal is to bring Rickshaw Art to a broader audience through creative communication, skills development and connections with new markets.”
“Dhaka’s Rickshaws and Rickshaw Painting” was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023.
Building on this recognition, UNESCO and Windmill Advertising Limited will work together to safeguard the history, aesthetics and cultural significance of Rickshaw Art while contributing to the social and economic advancement of associated artists.
Under the partnership, an integrated project titled “Rickshaw Painting: Expanding the Canvas” will be implemented.
The project will include training and skills development programs for artists, initiatives to expand the commercial potential of the art form, opportunities to connect artists with leading brands, and exhibitions and promotional activities to showcase the tradition to wider audiences.
The project also aims to highlight the creativity, stories and visual language reflected in Bangladesh’s Rickshaw Art while supporting artists’ livelihoods.
The MoU signing ceremony was attended by Kizzy Tahnin, Head of Culture, UNESCO Dhaka; Bipasha Tripura, Program Assistant, Culture; and Md Motiur Rahman Rabbi, Manager, Operation & Client Service, Windmill Advertising Limited.
Through the partnership, Windmill Advertising Limited’s experience in creative communication, public awareness, digital promotion and capacity development will complement UNESCO’s work to safeguard living cultural heritage.
The collaboration will also focus on documenting the knowledge and skills of artists and helping pass them on to future generations.

item.title: UNICEF, bKash partner to facilitate donations for children
item.description:
Donations to support children in Bangladesh are set to become easier and more accessible through a new collaboration between UNICEF and the country’s largest mobile financial services provider.
UNICEF announced the partnership with bKash on Wednesday as part of efforts to simplify the process of making contributions for children’s programs in Bangladesh.
The collaboration is expected to expand UNICEF’s fundraising initiatives by enabling more donors to contribute through bKash.
“Our collaboration with bKash, a trusted and widely used digital platform, enables UNICEF to connect with people and communities across Bangladesh through a simple, secure and accessible way to support children,” said Carla Haddad Mardini, Global Director, Private Fundraising and Partnerships, UNICEF.
“We are pleased to see this partnership come to fruition as part of UNICEF’s ongoing efforts to expand funding opportunities and mobilize durable support for children. Children are at the heart of Bangladesh’s future, and through this initiative, we can reach more of them with the services they need to survive, learn, and thrive. Every contribution, no matter the size, can help create lasting change in a child’s life and open the door to a brighter future,” she said.
Under the agreement, bKash users can donate directly to UNICEF through the bKash app by selecting the “Donations” option and then UNICEF.
Contributions can also be made through bKash’s offline merchant network, allowing wider participation in UNICEF’s mission to improve the lives of children.
Kamal Quadir, CEO of bKash, said: “At bKash, we are focused on creating impactful opportunities for community advancement. Having built the country's first digital donation platform, bKash empowers users to make informed decisions when contributing to meaningful causes. This partnership with UNICEF will bring strong momentum to fundraising initiatives aimed at building a brighter future for children.”
The agreement was signed last year in Dhaka in the presence of Carla Haddad Mardini, Global Director of UNICEF’s Private Fundraising and Partnerships, and Kamal Quadir, Chief Executive Officer of bKash.
As part of the collaboration, UNICEF will have a permanent presence in the donation section of the bKash app, increasing opportunities for organic contributions while enabling future awareness and fundraising initiatives.
All funds raised through the initiative will be used exclusively to support UNICEF’s programs for children in Bangladesh, including efforts to provide access to quality education and essential healthcare, protect children from violence and exploitation, and provide life-saving assistance during emergencies.
Each contribution will directly support initiatives aimed at helping children grow safe, healthy and full of hope.

item.title: Bangladesh, ICRC pledge deeper cooperation on humanitarian action
item.description:
Bangladesh and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) on Wednesday reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation on international humanitarian law and humanitarian action, including assistance to Rohingyas and host communities.
The commitment came during a meeting between State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir and ICRC Head of Delegation in Bangladesh Nicolas Fleury at the foreign ministry here, said a ministry press release.
Kobir appreciated the ICRC's longstanding humanitarian engagement in Bangladesh, particularly its contributions to promoting International Humanitarian Law (IHL), humanitarian assistance, disaster response, capacity-building and emergency support.
He reaffirmed Bangladesh's firm commitment to the Geneva Conventions and IHL, underscoring the important role of the National IHL Committee.
The state minister highlighted Bangladesh's contribution to promoting IHL globally, including as co-chair of the "IHL and Peace" workstream under the Global IHL Initiative.
He said the government was considering participation at an appropriate level in the "High-Level Conference on Humanity in War", scheduled to be held in Jordan in December this year.
Discussing the Rohingya situation, Kobir appreciated the ICRC's humanitarian assistance to the forcibly displaced Rohingyas and host communities in Cox's Bazar.
He urged the organization to strengthen its advocacy for the early repatriation of the Rohingyas to Myanmar, reiterating its essential role in global humanitarian affairs and international humanitarian law.
Fleury appreciated Bangladesh's continued cooperation and reaffirmed the ICRC's readiness to further support IHL capacity-building and humanitarian efforts in the country.
He also expressed commitment to further consolidating the longstanding partnership between Bangladesh and the ICRC.
